oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:title: Map of the British American Plantations (1754)
oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:description: "A map of the British American plantations, extending from Boston in New England to Georgia; including all the back settlements in the respective provinces as far as the Mississippi." An exceptional map of the American colonies and backcountry published in London at the time of the French & Indian War. It shows the territory of the "Cherakees" "Chikasas" and Upper Creeks with their towns and villages, including the site of "Tanase" from which the future state's name derived. On the Cumberland River is shown “Walkers Settlement 1750,” possibly a reference to the French Lick trading outpost and Dr. Thomas Walker’s 1750 exploration down the Cumberland. What was later called the Tennessee River is named the “Hugehego or Akansea R[iver]” on which an upstream “English Fort"—probably Fort Loudoun—is indicated.

Emanuel Bowen was an English map maker in the 18th century. He produced many well-known maps of the American colonies as well as county maps of England. His son was map maker Thomas Bowen. Two of his apprentices were renowned cartographers Thomas Kitchin and Thomas Jefferys. He served as geographer to King George II of England and Louis XV of France.

oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:title: Ashport to Memphis Confederate map
oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:description: This map showing Confederate military installations along the Tennessee portion of the Mississippi River was hand-drawn on linen by Albert Martin around 1861. It stretches from Ashport in the north to Memphis in the south and shows Confederate artillery batteries, with number, size and type of guns. Though detailed in its presentation of waterways, swamps, bluffs, plantations, certain landowners, and the numbered islands in the Mississippi River, its primary purpose was to depict the Confederate gun emplacements--Forts Harris, Randolph and Claiborn [sic: should be Cleburne for Col. Patrick R. Cleburne whose 1st Arkansas Regt. built the earthworks, later in the war called Fort Pillow]--protecting the river above Memphis early in the war. Troop deployments in the area are also indicated.

The importance of controlling this stretch of the Mississippi River was paramount for both sides during the Civil War, but especially for the Confederacy, which the great river divided. As indicated by this map, the Southern command had fortified the bluffs above Memphis with an array of heavy gun emplacements to guard against a potential Federal riverborne assault. Note the written comment that cotton bales and barricades were present in the streets of Memphis. Memphis would cease to function as a Confederate stronghold when it fell to Union forces on June 6, 1862.

oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:title: Route of the Memphis-Nashville-Bristol highway (1911)
oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:description: Map showing the proposed route of the Memphis-Nashville-Bristol Highway to be constructed 1911-1913. The map shows all the counties of Tennessee with their county seats, as well as the major railroads through Tennessee. There are advertisements bordering the map that show photographs of various road-building equipment. On the reverse is an open letter from the Wilson, Ingram and Company addressed to Mr. Good Road Builder, State of Tennessee, suggesting that Austin-Western Road Machinery be used.

The construction of the Memphis to Bristol Highway offered citizens, businesses, and tourists a means to effectively cross the state and offered the opportunity to unify more closely the three grand divisions. The good roads improvement movement had arisen in the 1890s with the support of the railroads, the farm alliances, and the bicyclists, and it had widespread public approval across the state. When motorized vehicles came onto the scene at the turn of the 19th century, they provided travel competition to railroads and steamboats and spawned the creation of local auto clubs and the Tennessee Good Roads Association. The Association threw its support behind the construction of an all-weather Memphis to Bristol highway. The building of the Memphis to Bristol Highway encouraged the undertaking of additional state road-building projects and encouraged Virginia and Mississippi to extend the highway. Local businessmen had formed the Memphis to Bristol Highway Association in 1911 to promote this 500-mile long highway. In 1926, two-thirds of the route was designated as U. S. 70, the major east-west corridor in the region. In the late 1920s the entire route became part of the Broadway of America Highway from California to New York.

oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:title: Nashville and the camp of the sixteenth regiment of Ills. Vols. Inft. at Edgefield, Tennessee
oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:description: A pictorial lithograph of Nashville and Edgefield during the Civil War, with the camp of the Illinois 16th Volunteer Infantry Regiment at Edgefield in the foreground. The Cumberland River is seen in the background with gunboats and riverboats depicted. The state capitol building can be seen in the background overlooking the city of Nashville. Structures featured within the camp are the guard house, the headquarters, the hospital, the sutler, a medical procedure, African American laborers, and the housing for the band.

The lithograph depicts camp activities as might be seen during the Civil War. The lithograph was created by Theodore Schrader of St. Louis, Missouri. The 16th Regiment Illinois Infantry was organized at Quincy, Illinois, and mustered in May 24, 1861. They marched from Tuscumbia, Alabama to Nashville from August 25 through September 15, 1862. They saw action at Columbia on September 10, 1862.

oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:title: Map of Tennessee (1818)
oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:description: This beautifully colored map of Tennessee constructed by John Melish from the surveys of John Strothers following the War of 1812. Shows early county lines and Indian boundaries prior to Jackson's Treaty and other cessions of Indian land after the war, along with some statistical and geological remarks. Western Tennessee is still Chickasaw territory, and the southeastern corner of the state is in Cherokee hands. Melish clearly was working remotely and had not been to Tennessee, as there are several fanciful mistakes such as the eastern tip of the state, the location of Reynoldsburg and the "Earthquake [Reelfoot] Lake," and numerous misspellings. Certain period features such as Fort Deposit, Southwest Point garrison, and the U.S. Agency for Cherokees are indicated.

John Melish was a Scottish-born cartographer who settled in the United States in 1811, after several previous visits. Melish came to dominate the map-making industry in this country and had a huge impact on the cartographic standards of his day.

oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:description: Hand-drawn map, done by an Illinois soldier who was present, of the Second Battle for Fort Donelson showing the location of artillery placements, breastworks, Union rifle pits, guard houses, Dover churches and town buildings, hospitals, cavalry quarters, and major roads and streams.

The Battle of Dover, also known as the Second Battle of Fort Donelson, took place February 3, 1863. Major General Joseph Wheeler led two cavalry brigades, one commanded by Nathan Bedford Forrest, to attack the 800-man garrison at Dover. The garrison, led by Colonel Abner C. Harding, was heavily entrenched and was able to hold off the Confederate assault until dusk. The following day Wheeler retreated, drawing the ire of Forrest, who vowed never again to serve under his command.

oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:description: Map depicting major features, especially roads, communities and railroads, present in Tennessee during the Civil War. A large detailed section of Kentucky occupies the top part of the map, and the states surrounding Tennessee receive fringe coverage. Counties are indicated in color, and major battle sites in Tennessee are underlined in red.

There are various editions of this map, but it was initially designed as a companion map to Lloyd's official map of the State of Kentucky. Being issued from the same plate, this does explain the appearance of almost all of Kentucky on this Tennessee map. James T. Lloyd and Company of New York and London was a popular map publisher of the day, often incorporating advertisements and testimonials. oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:title: Civil War map of the country traversed by the Nashville and Northwestern Railroad and the Nashville, Decatur and Stevenson Railroad
oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:description: Operational map drawn by Union topographical engineer Lt. Col. H. C. Wharton showing landowner's names, detailed road system, topography, mills, with notes as to land and road quality. Map covers a portion of Middle Tennessee west of Nashville covered by the Nashville and Northwestern Railroad, and south of Nashville following the Nashville, Decatur and Stevenson Railroad and the Duck River from Columbia to its mouth. Issued by command of Major General George H. Thomas. The map basically stretches from Nashville south to Columbia and west to the Tennessee River. The new Federal depot and supply installation at Johnsonville is shown. Scale is one half inch equals a mile. Color present along some railroad and water routes.

Wharton was a graduate of West Point who served with the U. S. Engineers as Chief Topographical Engineer in the Department of the Cumberland. Such detailed engineer's maps conveyed vital information to Federal troops entering an unfamiliar area, such as inhabitants' names, locations of mills, iron furnaces, blacksmith shops, and notations of good and bad roads and fords.

oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:title: State of Franklin map
oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:description: Early 20th century manuscript map of State of Franklin (Frankland), possibly drawn by J.T. McGill to accompany his article: ""Franklin and Frankland: Names and Boundaries,"" Tenn. Historical Magazine, v. 8, no. 4, (1925), p. 248.

This map seeks to distinguish between the geographic boundaries of the historic State of Franklin and the proposed state of Frankland. The State of Franklin, as McGill denotes on this map, existed from 1784 to 1788 and was formed from the area of Colonial North Carolina west of the mountains separating present-day Tennessee and North Carolina. Frankland, a rejected state proposal, was to encompass portions of Virginia, North Carolina, and Georgia, and possibly beyond. McGill also tackled the name issue in his article. Though it is contended that Frankland, "the land of free-men" was an early name applied in the new state proposals, the December 1784 Provisional Constitution of Jonesborough used "Franklin," and the Second Constitutional Convention at Greeneville in November of 1785 fixed the name of the state as "Franklin," in honor of Benjamin Franklin. Confusion over the years arose from historian John Haywood's insistence upon using "Frankland" when referring to the state and from the circulation of the printed rejected Houston Constitution of "Frankland," presumably authored largely by Dr. William Graham and Rev. Samuel Houston.

Robert Armstrong (1774-1849) was the Knox County surveyor appointed by Secretary of War John C. Calhoun to be US Surveyor for the 1819 Cherokee Treaty, for which task these maps were produced. oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:description: Drawn from French sources (Mr. D'Anville) and published in London in 1760, this map illustrates the colonial landscape of eastern North America and Canada at the time of the imperial struggle between France and England known as the Seven Year's War (French & Indian War). It is "Improved with the back settlements of Virginia and course of Ohio, illustrated with geographical and historical remarks." Map taken from between pages 134 and 135. Its chief value for Tennessee history lies in its depiction of the native Indian tribes, their settlements, colonial forts, rivers, etc. In the country of the "Cherakees" we find "Walkers Settlement 1750" on the "Cumberland or Shannoroens" River, the "Hogehege or Cherakees" [Tennessee] River, and many Cherokee towns, incl. "Tonase" which gave its name to the future state. In the country of the "Chikasaws" a "F[ort] Prudome [Prudhomme]" is shown near the future site of Memphis. The Creeks, "Chactaws" and other Southern tribes are shown.

oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:description: A map drawn by British Army Lt. Henry Timberlake in 1762 that identifies the Cherokee villages on the Little Tennessee River and includes a list of the number of warriors available from each village.

British Lt. Henry Timberlake traveled to the Overhill Cherokee villages on the Little Tennessee river in late 1761 to explain the treaty signed at Fort Robinson to the Cherokees located there. He remained with the Cherokee until March 1762, keeping a journal that was published in 1765 and contains a detailed account of Cherokee life as well as this map. He later accompanied several Cherokee headmen, including Attakullakulla, the Little Carpenter, to London to meet with King George.

oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:title: Abraham Bradley's Map of the United States (approximately 1796)
oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:description: A beautiful 18th century, paper-on-cloth map in color, "exhibiting the post-roads, the situations, connections & distances of the post-offices, stage roads, counties, ports of entry and delivery for foreign vessels, and the principal rivers" of North America. Includes the mail routes of North Carolina and the territory north of the Ohio (Northwest Territory), Cherokee country, west Florida, and "Tennassee" in its first year of statehood. Features such as Tennassee County (soon to be divided into Robertson and Montgomery counties), Old Fort Assumption, the Mero District, Fort Loudon, and the Cherokee towns of Chota, Chilhowee and Coyota are shown. The map depicts many military installations, native treaty lines and boundaries, iron works and furnaces, and a wealth of other historical data.

The map provides a detailed look at the post offices and postal routes of the Southern States, as they existed at the end of the 18th Century, locating every post office then in operation, as well as military installations, native treaty lines and boundaries, iron works and furnaces, and a wealth of other historical data. Abraham Bradley was a lawyer, judge, and assistant postmaster general. This copy is the 4th state of his 1796 first edition map of the postal routes of the United States, the first postal map ever produced in the United States.

oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:title: WW II Newsmap Vol. III No. 39F
oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:description: This Industrial Edition Newsmap from January, 1945 details the 161st week of U.S. participation in WW II. The largest map shows the Allied counter-offensive to the Battle of the Bulge, one of the last German offensive campaigns of the war. The small map to the left shows the Allied offensive in Burma against Japanese forces.The map located in the bottom center shows Allied landings on the Philippine islands of Mindoro and Marinduque. The map in the top right shows the American invasion of the Philippine island of Luzon. Accompanying the maps are a collection of photographs that show the American war effort, from military action and supplies to some light-hearted distractions from the hostilities.

TSLA holds a large collection of these WWII "newsmaps," detailing for the American public the weekly events of US military efforts in Europe and the Pacific theaters. The Bureau of Public Relations was established in the Office of the Secretary of War in February 1941.The Bureau served as the central War Department agency to determine policies and procedures for disseminating military information to the public. After August 1942, it was also responsible for the public relations activities of the Army Air Forces, the Army Service Forces and the Army Ground Forces. During the war, the Bureau produced these weekly newsmaps for War Department distribution.

oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:title: George A. Washington's Wessyngton Plantation and Land, Robertson County, Tenn. (1868)
oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:description: Hand-drawn and colored map of George A. Washington's land including the Wessyngton plantation, surveyed by Felix A. Harris in the 1860s. The map shows farm tracts with metes and bounds, fields, springs, houses, gristmill, possibly tenant houses, churches, and many neighboring houses along Sulphur Fork Creek in Robertson County. Wessyngton was one of the largest dark-fired tobacco producers in the United States during the 19th century; it had a sizeable antebellum enslaved population, many of whom remained on the farm after the Civil War as sharecroppers.

One of the largest tobacco plantations of the South, Wessyngton was the estate of the Washington family, one of the state's largest enslavers. In 1860 the family owned 13,000 acres and enslaved 274 people.

Details include outlines of each building, the location of windows and doors, property boundaries, firewalls, types of building materials used, heat sources, light sources and electric, locations of fire hydrants, location of water and gas mains, etc.

Daniel Alfred Sanborn, a civil engineer and surveyor, began working on fire insurance maps in the 1860s and his company soon became one of the largest and most successful American map companies. Sanborn's first work mapping cities for insurance purposes began in Tennessee when Aetna Insurance hired him to survey a few towns across the state, however none of these earliest examples are known to exist today (Ristow, Walter W. "United States Fire Insurance and Underwriters Maps· 1852—1968." The Quarterly Journal of the Library of Congress 25, no. 3 (1968): 194-218." Sanborn maps were originally created to estimate fire insurance risks. Insurance companies would decide how much insurance, if any, was to be offered to a customer solely through the use of a Sanborn map. Today, the maps are frequently used for historical research and for preservation and restoration purposes.

oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:title: Hand-drawn plats showing location of 18th century land grants west of Nashville, Tennessee
oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:description: Samuel Weakley's plat map shows early land claims and "pre-emptions" along Richland Creek near its junction with the Cumberland River west of Nashville, Tenn. (Pre-emptions were 640-acre tracts granted by North Carolina to original settlers who had taken the considerable risk to come to the Cumberland and make improvements on the land.) Additional information about each plot is shown including: owner, date of acquisition, acreage, and border markers. Included is the land and homeplace on Richland Creek of James Robertson, one of the founders of Nashville and leader of the early Cumberland settlements. Also shown are the pre-emption grants of John and Daniel Dunham, elements of which eventually made up parts of Belle Meade plantation.

Samuel Anderson Weakley was a chief in the operation division of the U.S. Corps of Engineers in Nashville, Tenn. as well as a genealogist. He did careful deed research to produce his plats of early North Carolina land grants, which can be found in TSLA's collection of his papers. He assembled the greater part of his research into a book, "The Southern Virginia Weakley Families and Their Descendents," also available at the Library & Archives.

The Dutch trading concession, where Westerners were allowed to trade, is also depicted. Also attached is the envelope in which the map was originally stored. This map was an early gift to the Tennessee Historical Society and came with the following inscription: ""This map is all the work of native artists, and was printed and colored in the City of Jeddo, Japan for the Rev. Henry Wood, Chaplain of the steam frigate Powhatan."" Rev. Wood evidently served as chaplain with Commodore Matthew Perry's second fleet that sailed into Tokyo Bay in 1854 to force the opening of Tokugawa Shogunate Japan to Western, i.e. American, commerce. oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:title: States of America
oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:description: This London-published color map reflects twenty "States of America," each marked with a Roman numeral. An 1840 reprint of an 1823 publication, the map actually reflects an earlier period in the nation's history with its labeling of territories, Indian tribes, and East Tennessee as "Franklinia" (a reference to the frontier-era State of Franklin). Noted on the map are cities and towns; rivers and major waterways; and Indian towns including Creek and Cherokee settlements. The map reaches north into Canada, south to the Gulf of Mexico, east to the North Atlantic Ocean, and west to Louisiana.

This rather fanciful depiction of the early United States--e.g. Indiana is shown east of Ohio--is interesting for what it tells us about the state of English knowledge about the former American colonies. In Tennessee, "Franklinia" refers to the attempt made by the inhabitants of North Carolina's trans-Appalachian counties of Washington, Sullivan, and Greene to form the independent "State of Franklin" from 1784 to 1788 and illustrates the lasting memory of this experiment in self-government.

oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:title: Map of East Tennessee and western North Carolina showing mineral deposits (1876)
oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:description: The map shows primarily East Tennessee ("vicinity of Knoxville") and western North Carolina, as well as small portions of northern Georgia, southwestern Virginia, and southeastern Kentucky. It is extremely detailed as to the commercial mining industries of East Tennessee, showing mineral deposits, marble quarries, coal mines and salt works throughout the region, specifically identifying copper and iron ores in color. Iron forges and furnaces are also indicated, as well as stream names, coves, local peaks and their elevation. The map also shows railroads; completed, in construction, and proposed.

This map is an artifact of Tennessee's effort to promote the rich mineral resources available for potential manufacturers after the Civil War. At the time, northern investors were purchasing huge acreages in mineral rich areas of Appalachia. Tennessee was an early leader in iron and--to a lesser extent--steel production as well as coal mining. However, by the beginning of the 20th century, the focus of steel-making shifted southward to Birmingham, Alabama. Charles Waring & Co. was a civil engineering, drafting, and surveying firm in Knoxville, Tennessee in the latter half of the 19th century.

oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:title: Map of British governments in North America (1763)
oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:description: Published in London in 1763, this map interprets the landscape of the North American colonies following Great Britain's victory over France in the Seven Year's War. Specifically, it shows the line laid down on the crest of the Appalachian Mountains by the Proclamation of 1763, beyond which American colonists' westward encroachment onto Native American lands was prohibited. The British Crown's limit on westward expansion in favor of "Lands Reserved for the Indians" was one of the American colonists' chief complaints leading to the Revolution.

The Royal Proclamation of 1763 was issued by King George III, following the conclusion of the French and Indian War (Seven Years' War). As a result of their defeat in the war, France ceded much of its North American territory to Great Britain. The proclamation outlined the management of the newly acquired French colonies as well as regulated colonial expansion west of the Appalachian Mountains.

oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:title: Geological map of state of Tennessee (1855)
oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:description: A color-coded geological map of Tennessee showing rock formations, commercial deposits and mines, and iron-making operations across the state. Executed by James Safford, Tennessee's state geologist before the Civil War, it details the locations of mineral deposits, iron furnaces, forges and bloomeries, mills, coal mines, and marble quarries. It particularly names all the places associated with the iron industry in the Western Highland Rim and East Tennessee, one of the state's key economic sectors during the antebellum era. Along the bottom is a geological cross section of the state with a rough elevation projection. The top right corner contains an enlarged map of the copper mines around Ducktown in the southeastern corner of Polk County, Tenn.

James M. Safford was a chemist, geologist, and professor in Tennessee. He studied chemistry at Yale, and taught geology, chemistry, and botany at the University of Nashville, Cumberland University, and Vanderbilt University. He served as State Geologist for the much of the latter half of the 19th century, and his geological survey of Tennessee in 1869 is still cited in the field today. He and J. B. Killebrew published a report on the agricultural and mineral resources of Tennessee which served as the basis for textbooks, pamphlets, essays, and bulletins for decades thereafter.

oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:title: Battle lines positions map, part of the master plan for Fort Donelson National Military Park
oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:description: National Park Service map, showing the battle lines of the positions on February 14, 1862, to be used as part of the plans for the Fort Donelson National Military Park at Dover, Tenn. Map shows Confederate and Union positions relative to landmarks present in 1940 such as the national cemetery and the park headquarters. There are also hand-written notes showing proposed locations for a museum and monument.

The Battle of Fort Donelson began on February 12, 1862, just days after the surrender of nearby Fort Henry. Union forces under Brigadier General Ulysses S. Grant surrounded the fort's defenses, commanded by Brigadier General John B. Floyd. Confederate troops under Brigadier General Gideon J. Pillow attempted to push back the right flank to create an escape route to Nashville, but were repulsed by a counterattack commanded by Brigadier General Lew Wallace. After the unsuccessful push, Floyd and Pillow fled, passing command to Brigadier General Simon Bolivar Buckner. Colonel Nathan Bedford Forrest refused to surrender and escaped to Nashville with his cavalry overnight. Buckner surrendered the fort and over 12,000 troops to Grant the following day, February 16. Fort Donelson was the last major obstacle on the way to Nashville and opened up Middle Tennessee to Union control. The battle led to Grant's promotion to Major General, while Floyd was relieved of his command and Pillow was suspended for two months.

oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:title: Revolutionary war-era map of the southern colonies
oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:description: This hand-drawn map depicts the Old Southwest frontier, possibly around 1778, according to a pencilled inscription. The boundary between Virginia and North Carolina is drawn, as is the trans-Mississippi River "Bounds of Virginia & New England" and a northern boundary of the Georgia colony. The map details many French and English forts as well as the location of Native American tribes and settlements across the region. Numerous Cherokee towns are depicted with particular care, and the Tennessee River is named the "Hogohege [or] Cherokees R." It appears that the first Anglo-American settlement in the Tennessee country--Watauga or "Vatoga"--is also depicted.

Though the provenance of this map is unclear, it does belong to some of the earliest papers collected by the Tennessee Historical Society or its predecessor, the Tennessee Antiquarian Society. It may have been drawn by one of the surviving Cumberland settlers, since it uses very dated mid-18th century place-names and French colonial spellings for a number of sites.

oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:title: Civil War maps of the 1863 Chattanooga campaign and the Red River expedition in Louisiana
oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:description: Plate L of the Atlas to Accompany the Official Records of the Union and Confederate Armies, 1861-1865, containing six small maps relating to battles and troop positions during the Civil War. Five of the maps are of the Chattanooga area during the late 1863 campaign while the sixth is from the Red River expedition in Louisiana in 1864. The detailed maps are complete with troop placement, battle lines and geographic details such as rivers, streams, roads, railroads. Clockwise from bottom left: Battle of Lookout Mountain; Country in Vicinity of Brown's Ferry; Battlefield of Missionary Ridge; Positions of Second Division, Fourth Army Corps; Red River Expedition; Chattanooga and Vicinity.

Following their victory at the Battle of Chickamauga, General Braxton Bragg's Army of Tennessee chased Union forces under Major General William Rosecrans to Chattanooga. The Union settled behind the defenses in the city, while the Confederates occupied the surrounding high ground. Major General Ulysses S. Grant was given command of Federal forces in the western theater, and was joined with reinforcements. On October 27, the Union were able to open a "Cracker Line" at Brown's Ferry to resupply their troops. After small battles at Wauhatchie and Orchard Knob, Major General Joseph Hooker launched an assault, overrunning Confederate positions on Lookout Mountain on November 24th, just in time to assist Grant's advance on Bragg's position at Missionary Ridge. The result was a resounding victory for the Union, crushing the Confederates' hopes that emerged from their victory at Chickamauga. Chattanooga became the supply center for General William T. Sherman's Atlanta Campaign.

Iron ore has been one of Tennessee's most important natural resources since the 1790's. Tennessee was ranked third nationally in iron bloomery production in 1860, with Lewis County being amongst the leaders in the state. A small print of the church is included in the bottom left-hand corner.

On the night of March 30, 1890, the Cumberland Presbyterian Church of Fosterville, Tennessee was destroyed by a "cyclone." The church was insured for lightning damage only by the Equitable Insurance Company of Nashville. The insurance company refused to pay for damages, arguing that the church was destroyed by a cyclone, not lightning.

oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:description: Antebellum nautical map showing the navigational approaches to Charleston harbor. The United States Coast Survey can trace its roots to an act signed into law by President Thomas Jefferson in 1807 to generate maritime charts for the newly formed nation. Ferdinand Hassler was selected as the first superintendent in 1816 and served until the jurisdiction of the survey was moved under the control of the Army in 1818. He was reappointed superintendent by President Andrew Jackson in 1832 with the department once again under civilian control. The Coast Survey created nautical charts, performed hydrographic surveys, as well as executed the first studies of the Gulf Stream. Known as the United States Coast and Geodetic Survey beginning in 1878, the department provided much needed work for engineers during the Great Depression and helped create maps and charts for the Allies in World War II. In 1970, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration was formed and was given control over the agency.

Coal mining in Tennessee first began in the 1840s. However, it did not become an important industry until after the Civil War, when railroad construction made it easier for miners to reach deposits and for coal to reach cities. In the 1870s, Tennessee was tenth in bituminous, or soft, coal production, with output primarily in plateau counties. Around this time, investors purchased huge tracts of land and controlled the most fruitful mines. From 1909 to 1939, coal was the most valuable mineral resource in Tennessee. Production burgeoned during World War II and again in the 1970s, topping out at 11.2 million tons in 1972. During this time, Tennessee ranked eleventh nationally in production, but by the 1990s the value of coal production had fallen by approximately 66%.

"Our village was the scene of a very sad and exciting affair last Saturday evening, the particulars of which, as near as we can learn them, being as follows: Mr. Will T. Erwin and Lew Adkinson had a trial before Esq. Sparkman during which, Roan Erwin and Lew Adkinson got into a fight, Adkinson being very much bruised in the face with a piece of iron in the hands of Erwin. A short time after, a dispute arose in the street between Ped Fitzgerald and Roan Erwin, when Will T. Erwin stepped up and told Fitzgerald to dry up, who immediately took up a large rock and threw at Erwin, who dodged, and drawing his pistol, fired, the ball striking Fitzgerald in the left breast, near the heart, and passed through and out at the right side of the back. Fitzgerald spoke but once and fell dead. Erwin was arrested after a short struggle, by P. C. Gray who was near at the time. Had Erwin's pistol fired for him the second time, Gray would also have been a corpse, but an overruling Providence prevented the double tragedy. Erwin was tried before Esq. John T. Sparkman and admitted to bail in the sum of $3,500, J. L. Williams, F. B. Craige, and C. S. Erwin as bondsmen. Fitzgerald leaves a wife and six small children, and a widowed mother. Too much whisky was the cause of this sad affair. 'Tis very strange that our country cannot afford temperance men enough to give us some kind of law to prevent such foul deeds. Cursed alcohol! Will its ravages never grow less? It makes so many poor widows and orphans, and all classes feel its plagues." -The Columbia Herald (Columbia, Tenn.) May 30, 1873

oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:title: Map showing the Mexico City Campaign during the Mexican War (1847)
oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:description: Extremely detailed map showing Gen. Winfield Scott's Mexico City campaign during the Mexican War, Aug.-Sept. 1847. It outlines Mexican and American troop dispositions and movements during the three major battles around Mexico City: Contreras, Churubusco, and Molino del Rey (the fortress at Chapultepec). It details the topography and nineteenth century road system around the Mexican capital, city grids, forts, roads, canals, and geographic features such as rivers, lakes, and the "Pedregal or field of lava" near Contreras over which attacking American troops moved. The upper right and left hand corners show the number of casualties in each of the battles at the end of this campaign.

On March 9, 1847, American troops performed their first major amphibious operation, landing 12,000 men, supplies, weapons, and horses at Veracruz, Mexico. After the 12-day siege of the city, the Mexicans surrendered. Scott's troops continued their campaign toward Mexico City and met Mexican troops under General Santa Anna entrenched near Cerro Gordo. After a decisive victory, the Americans marched on to Puebla, who surrendered without resistance. After the Battles of Contreras, Churubusco, Molino del Rey, and Chapultepec, Santa Anna withdrew to Guadalupe Hidalgo. After a 5 month guerilla campaign, the war ended there with the signing of the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo on February 2, 1848. The treaty ceded California, Nevada, Utah, and parts of New Mexico, Arizona, Texas, Oklahoma, Kansas, Wyoming, and Colorado to the United States for $15 million. Many generals in the Civil War participated in the Mexican War, specifically the Mexico City campaign including: Robert E. Lee, George Meade, Ulysses S. Grant, James Longstreet, Thomas "Stonewall" Jackson, Gideon J. Pillow, Joseph E. Johnston, Sterling Price, George B. McClellan, Daniel H. Hill, and George Pickett. Future Tennessee governor William Trousdale served as a Colonel in this campaign.

oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:title: Map of Columbia (Tenn.) showing the 1946 'Operation Mink Slide.'
oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:description: The blueprint map of Columbia was originally published in 1937 by C. J. Akin. This copy belonged to Tennessee State Guard commander Major General Jacob McGavock Dickinson, Jr.and was originally part of his manuscript collection, the Dickinson, Jacob McGavock (1851-1928) Papers 1812-1946. It was used by him in the Guard's policing actions during the Columbia Race Riot in 1946. He (or someone on his staff) drew on the map using wax pencil, denoting certain roadblocks, military cordons, barracks, and unit placement throughout the town as the State Guard tried to seal off the African American neighborhoods and get between the two sides. The State Guard played a generally positive role in calming the white mob, keeping them away from the guns in the armory, and cordoning off the African American neighborhoods and "Mink Slide" business district.

The 1946 Columbia "race riot"--more accurately, white mob violence and near-lynching--was significant mainly for the self-defense role played by black veterans of World War II and the legal defense mounted by NAACP attorneys such as Z. Alexander Looby and Thurgood Marshall. In Maury County racial tension ran high, with three lynchings in the years before this episode. Between 1877 and 1950 nearly 4,000 African Americans were lynched in the South, 225 of them in Tennessee. [Equal Justice Initiative report published in Washington Post, 2/10/15] On February 25, Navy veteran James Stephenson and his mother walked into to a downtown store to pick up a repaired radio. The white clerk and Mrs. Stephenson began arguing over the order when the clerk struck her. James intervened and struggled with the clerk--who crashed through a store window. The Stephensons were arrested, paid a fine, and were released. The situation escalated when the clerk's father accused Stephenson of assault with intent to commit murder. Stephenson was arrested again. [C. V. West, Tennessee Encyclopedia of History and Culture] Tension accelerated that night when an angry white crowd assembled at the courthouse. In the African American business district, nicknamed the Mink Slide, black citizens--some of them veterans--also gathered. Four local (white) policemen entered Mink Slide after disregarding warnings from the black community to stop. Shots were fired, and the officers were wounded. Patrolmen from the Tennessee Highway Patrol (THP) entered the city, and in the early morning hours of February 26 patrolmen and whites surrounded the black district. They looted Mink Slide, illegally searched homes, fired indiscriminately into buildings, and confiscated weapons. Dozens were arrested but denied bail and legal counsel. [West, TEHC) The "riot" drew national attention. The NAACP sent attorneys Thurgood Marshall and Walter White to Nashville to assemble a legal team. Z. Alexander Looby and Maurice Weaver assisted with the jailed men's defense. The situation worsened on February 28 when two black men were killed and one was wounded while in THP custody. Circumstances were suspicious, but the killings were the last spasm of violence in Columbia. Most of the black defendants were cleared of charges; although harsh THP reaction was considered by an all-white federal grand jury, the patrolmen were ultimately cleared.

This map depicts the terrain of the famous 1892 Coal Creek Rebellion, one of the earliest actions of American miners against the use of leased convicts to break strikes in the coal fields.

oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:description: Map of Central America drawn for the Senate Foreign Relations Committee in 1856. Prospective railroad routes, treaty boundary lines, and ancient Mayan ruins such as Palenque are shown.

This map was created by the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, possibly in response to the filibustering movement that occurred in the 1850s. In 1856, William Walker, a native Nashvillian, managed to take over Nicaragua with a small expeditionary force. The surrounding countries were unhappy with his usurpation and reinstatement of slavery and formed a coalition to oust him. This coalition was successful and Walker returned to the United States. After a couple of subsequent failed expeditions to the region, he was captured by the British and turned over to Honduran authorities who executed him in 1860.

oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:description: This hand-drawn survey shows the proposed location of Bell County and Nashoba County, Tennessee. The map displays county borders, both old and new state borders, cities within the proposed county, county seats, the Memphis and Charleston Railroad, and clearly lists the scale used in the creation of the map. A rudimentary drawing of the Tennessee and Mississippi Rivers flank the survey.

A flurry of new counties were proposed after the State Constitution of 1870, due to the reduction of size and population thresholds for creation. Bell and Nashoba counties, in southwestern Tennessee, were among those that were proposed but never established. Bell County was proposed by an act of the state legislature on December 20, 1870, created from the southern sections of Fayette, Hardeman, and McNairy counties. However, the commissioners of the existing counties did not relinquish the land so easily. Running through the middle of the proposed county was the Memphis and Charleston Railroad, which to these rural counties was an important source of tax revenue. At least two court cases were filed to quash the formation of this new county. The Tennessee Supreme Court heard these, and in the case Thomas H. Cocke et al v. John G. Gooch et al, Justice, and future Tennessee governor, Peter Turney sided with the commissioners of the existing counties, barring the creation of this new domain.

It is named for Revolutionary War hero General Jethro Sumner. Its county seat is Gallatin, named for U.S. Treasury Secretary, Albert Gallatin, while its largest city today is Hendersonville, named for early settler William Henderson and shown on this map from its days as a small village.

oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:title: Surveys of John Walker Jr. and Elizabeth Lowry land in Marion County, Tennessee and Cherokee territory (1820)
oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:description: Two surveys of 640 acre 'reservations' are included in this document. Such tracts were granted to tribal heads of families "residing within the ceded territory" of land in southeastern Tennessee, conveyed by the Cherokee to the United States by the 1819 treaty. The first is of Elizabeth Lowry's (Lowery) land (640 acres) on the north side of the Tennessee River in Marion County, incl. her dwelling house. The second is of John Walker Jr.'s land (640 acres) on the north side of the Tennessee River in Cherokee territory, incl. his dwelling house and ferry. This plat is accompanied by a letter to Col. Return J. Meigs, the Cherokee agent, stating his residency. A third, text-only survey for Elizabeth "Betsey" Pack is included.

John Walker Jr.'s father, John Walker Sr., was half Cherokee, a friend of Andrew Jackson by virtue of fighting under him during the Creek Wars, including Horseshoe Bend, and grandson of Nancy Ward. John Walker Jr. was the son of John Walker Sr. and Elizabeth Lowery. He married Emily Stanfield Meigs, Col. Return J. Meigs grand-daughter, and Nannie Bushyhead, sister of Reverend Jesse Bushyhead. Walker was eventually shot and killed by men who opposed letting the Cherokee remain in Tennessee and parts of Georgia.

oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:title: Washington County, Tennessee (1828)
oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:description: This hand-drawn map of Washington County from 1828 shows cities, roads, ferries, residences, churches, mills, and county lines. Geographic features include rivers, creeks, mountains, and coves. Elijah and Elihu Embree's forge and furnace are shown in "Bumper's (Bumpass) Cove," where they mined and smelted lead and iron. Washington College, Salem Church, a Baptist meeting house, and a plough factory are denoted on the map, as are numerous named ferries and mills. The chief purpose of the map, in fact, seems to be locating the water-powered mills and manufactories of Washington County.

Washington County is Tennessee's oldest county, organizing itself as the Washington District in the early 1770s until it was annexed by North Carolina and officially dubbed Washington County in 1777. It was a part of the failed State of Franklin in the 1780s, and the territory south of the River Ohio in the 1790s, before ultimately joining Tennessee after admittance to the Union in 1796. It is named for General and President George Washington. Its county seat is Jonesborough, named for North Carolina statesman Willie Jones, while its largest city is Johnson City, is named for an early settler, Henry Johnson. Johnson City briefly changed its name to Haynesville during the Civil War to honor Confederate senator Landon Carter Haynes.

oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:title: Survey of Pathkiller's land on south side of the Tennessee River at his ferry
oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:description: Robert Armstrong's 1819 survey for a Cherokee chief, "the Pathkiller," on the south side of the Tennessee River at his ferry. Plat and surveyor's description of 640 acre tract. Such 'reservations' were granted to tribal heads of families "residing within the ceded territory" of land in southeastern Tennessee, conveyed by the Cherokee to the United States by the 1819 treaty. David Taylor and Taylor Eldridge served as chain carriers. Plat also shows Pathkiller's dwelling house adjacent to ferry.

Pathkiller was the last hereditary chief of the Cherokee. He fought the Overmountain Men and other Watauga frontiersmen with Dragging Canoe in the Cherokee-American Wars. He served as a colonel under Andrew Jackson in the Creek Wars, including at Horseshoe Bend. A full-blooded Native American, he was the Principal Chief of the Cherokee Nation from 1811-1827. This land was the subject of multiple Tennessee Supreme Court cases between Pathkiller and John Blair.

oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:description: Map of western France, and parts of Germany, Italy, Belgium, Netherlands, and Luxembourg during the Napoleonic Wars. Geographic features such as mountains, rivers, lakes, channels, and oceans are indicated. An inset of Malta is included with a description of General Napoleon Bonaparte's capture of the island. This is a detailed French map of Central Europe near the height of Napoleon's military conquests.

Jacques Esnauts and Michel Rapilly ran a printing and publishing firm in Paris in the 18th Century. They were the originators of colored fashion plates for men and women, producing a collection known as Galerie des Modes et costumes Francais. The pair printed maps as well, including plans of Paris and other French cities, and maps of America during the Revolutionary War. Rapilly died in 1797 and Esnauts continued to produce maps such as this one until his death in 1813.

oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:title: Scotland, drawn and engrav'd from a series of angles and astronomical observations (1800)
oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:description: This extremely detailed map of Scotland from the end of the 18th century shows towns, cities, and roads. Geographic features such as hills, mountains, rivers, and lakes are indicated. The legend denotes borough towns which send members to Parliament, market towns, parish towns, seats and noted houses, Ancient Roman and Celtic ruins,roads and camps are shown, as are turnpike roads, castles, military roads, bens (mountains), country roads, lochs, rivers and burns, hills, and a distance table. Historic Roman names for certain features are written in separate font. Each county is outlined by watercolor. Thousands of family and place names from the 1700s are indicated on this map, making it highly useful for Scottish genealogy.

John Ainslie was a Scottish surveyor and cartographer active in the late 18th and early 19th centuries. He was born in Jedburgh, Scotland in 1745 and educated at the Jedburgh Grammar School. He served as an apprentice to the Geographer to King George III, Thomas Jefferys. Ainslie returned to Scotland and began work on surveying and mapping Scottish counties and islands. From 1787 to 1789 he worked on his groundbreaking map of Scotland, the most accurate of its time. In 1812 he published A Comprehensive Treatise on Land Surveying comprising the Theory and Practice of all its Branches, one of the preeminent surveying works of the time. Ainslie died in Edinburgh in 1828.

The United States Coast Survey can trace its roots to an act signed into law by President Thomas Jefferson in 1807 to generate maritime charts for the newly formed nation. Ferdinand Hassler was selected as the first superintendent in 1816 and served until the jurisdiction of the survey was moved under the control of the Army in 1818. He was reappointed superintendent by President Andrew Jackson in 1832 with the department once again under civilian control. The Coast Survey created nautical charts, performed hydrographic surveys, as well as executed the first studies of the Gulf Stream. Known as the United States Coast and Geodetic Survey beginning in 1878, the department provided much needed work for engineers during the Great Depression and helped create maps and charts for the Allies in World War II. In 1970, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration was formed and was given control over the agency.

The United States Coast Survey can trace its roots to an act signed into law by President Thomas Jefferson in 1807 to generate maritime charts for the newly formed nation. Ferdinand Hassler was selected as the first superintendent in 1816 and served until the jurisdiction of the survey was moved under the control of the Army in 1818. He was reappointed superintendent by President Andrew Jackson in 1832 with the department once again under civilian control. The Coast Survey created nautical charts, performed hydrographic surveys, as well as executed the first studies of the Gulf Stream. Known as the United States Coast and Geodetic Survey beginning in 1878, the department provided much needed work for engineers during the Great Depression and helped create maps and charts for the Allies in World War II. In 1970, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration was formed and was given control over the agency.

oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:title: Geologic Atlas of the United States. Columbia Folio Tennessee
oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:description: 16-page folio describing the geology of Columbia (Tenn." Contents include descriptive text, topographic map, areal geology map, economic geology map, silurian embayment map, structure section sheet, columnar section sheet, correlation sheet, faunal chart, and illustration sheet.

The USGS was established in 1879 to classify public lands and examine geology and mineral resources. A major concept was to create a Geologic Atlas of the United States which would be made up of folios, each containing topographical, geological, and other illustrations and text describing a particular quadrangle. Eventually, making the folios became too expensive and the last one was produced in 1945 and the atlas abandoned. USGS mapping still exists today for the purposes of practical land-use problems, such as ground-water studies, earthquake, volcano, landslide, and flooding monitoring, and urban development.

oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:title: Totopotomoy
oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:description: Map of Totopotomoy, Virginia showing roads, railroads, landowners names, the Virginia Central Railroad, the Pamunkey River, and topography. Troop positions are shown with Union forces in blue and Confederate forces in red. Surveyed and drawn by Major J.E. Weyss, assisted by F. Theilkuhl, J. Strasser and G. Thompson.

The Battle of Totopotomoy Creek was fought in May 1864 between Union Lieutenant General Ulysses S. Grant and Confederate General Robert E. Lee. Following the Battle of North Anna, Grant's troops moved south to the Pamunkey River. Lee's troops were entrenched at Totopotomoy Creek. Grant was able to fend off the Confederates and continue south to Cold Harbor, which would result in one of the deadliest battles of the Civil War.

oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:title: The Wilderness
oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:description: Detailed map of The Wilderness (northern Virginia) showing roads, mills, mines, an unfinished railroad, the Wilderness Tavern, and the Rapidan River. Troop positions are shown with Union forces in blue and Confederate forces in red. Surveyed and drawn by Major J. E. Weyss, assisted by F. Theilkuhl, J. Strasser and G. Thompson.

The Battle of the Wilderness, part of Gen. Grant's Overland Campaign, was fought on May 5 to May 7, 1864. The inconclusive battle saw 125,000 Union soldiers assault the wooded defensive position of Lee's Army of Northern Virginia, numbering about 65,000. The forest provided some cover from Grant's superior artillery. Grant's attack on May 6 and Longstreet's counterattack on May 7 resulted in 17,666 Union casualties and 11,033 Confederate casualties. On May 7, Grant decided to move the move southeast to better terrain to better utilize his numerical advantage.
oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:creator: Michler, N (Nathaniel), 1827-1881

oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:title: The Harbor of Annapolis
oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:description: Map showing the hydrographic details of the Harbor of Annapolis. Relief shown by hachures. Depths shown by soundings and shading. Includes sailing directions, tide information, notes, and U.S. Coast Survey Office insignia.

The United States Coast Survey can trace its roots to an act signed into law by President Thomas Jefferson in 1807 to generate maritime charts for the newly formed nation. Ferdinand Hassler was selected as the first superintendent in 1816 and served until the jurisdiction of the survey was moved under the control of the Army in 1818. He was reappointed superintendent by President Andrew Jackson in 1832 with the department once again under civilian control. The Coast Survey created nautical charts, performed hydrographic surveys, as well as executed the first studies of the Gulf Stream. Known as the United States Coast and Geodetic Survey beginning in 1878, the department provided much needed work for engineers during the Great Depression and helped create maps and charts for the Allies in World War II. In 1970, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration was formed and was given control over the agency.

oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:title: The Chattanooga Campaign of August and September 1863
oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:description: Shows the Chattanooga campaign of August and September 1863. It was enlarged from a map compiled in 1865 by C. S. Mergell. The map is complete with troop movements, battle lines and geographic details such as rivers, streams, roads, railroads. Labeled as Map No. 5.

Following their victory at the Battle of Chickamauga, General Braxton Bragg’s Army of Tennessee chased Union forces under Major General William Rosecrans to Chattanooga. The Union settled behind the defenses in the city, while the Confederates occupied the surrounding high ground. Major General Ulysses S. Grant was given command of Federal forces in the western theater, and was joined with reinforcements. On October 27, the Union were able to open a “Cracker Line” at Brown’s Ferry to resupply their troops. After small battles at Wauhatchie and Orchard Knob, Major General Joseph Hooker launched an assault, overrunning Confederate positions on Lookout Mountain on November 24th, just in time to assist Grant’s advance on Bragg’s position at Missionary Ridge. The result was a resounding victory for the Union, crushing the Confederates' hopes that emerged from their victory at Chickamauga. Chattanooga became the supply center for General William T. Sherman’s Atlanta Campaign.
oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:creator: United States. Army. Corps of Engineers; Von Glümer, J.

oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:description: Early map of Tennessee published in Arrowsmith and Lewis's 1804 atlas. It depicts Tennessee at statehood, before the division of Tennessee County into Montgomery and Robertson. The primary function of this map was to inform travelers and settlers of state's river system and topography. Other features include courthouses, Southwest Point, Ross's Iron Works, cities, towns, and some annotations as to the ground. A section of present-day northern Alabama is labeled Tennessee Company, a land speculation venture. Relief shown by hachures.

He worked for the American Encyclopedia for a time, before revising Adrian Balbi's Atlas Designed to Illustrate the Abridgement of Universal Geography, Modern & Ancient. oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:title: Surveys of William Brown's and David Field's land both on north side of the Tennessee River
oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:description: Two surveys on this document. The first is a 640 acre survey of David Fields' land on the north side of the Tennessee River near an island, possibly Williams Island. The second is a 640 acre survey of William Brown's land on the north side of the Tennessee River about a mile below the mouth of North Chickamauga Creek. It states it is a small distance above a large boiling spring.

Sgt. William Brown and David Fields were Cherokee who received reservations from the United States government after the Treaty of 1819. Both fought in the Creek War, including at the Battle of Horseshoe Bend under John Brown, a Cherokee officer. William Brown was severely wounded during the battle.

John Spears (Speers) and Lewis Ross were Cherokee who received reservations from the United States government after the Treaty of 1819. Both fought in the Creek Wars, including at the Battle of Horseshoe Bend. John Spears was an officer in the Cherokee regiment and Lewis Ross was general staff. Lewis Ross is the brother of famous Cherokee chief John Ross.

oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:title: Survey of John Ross land along the Tennessee River
oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:description: Survey of 640 acres of land given to John Ross, as per the Cherokee Treaty of 1819, along the Tennessee River, shows island in the river. James Carrouth and Jonathan Kerkendall served as chain carriers.

John Ross is one of the most famous of the later Cherokee Chiefs. He was only part Cherokee, but readily identified with them. He fought in the Creek Wars under Andrew Jackson, including the Battle of Horseshoe Bend as general staff, reaching the rank of lieutenant. He served as assistant to Col. Meigs in the Indian Agency. He and Timothy Meigs founded Ross's Landing in 1816, later known as Chattanooga. After the death of Pathkiller in 1827, he was selected as Principal Chief of the Cherokee Nation. Ross ardently defended against Cherokee removal in the 1830s, but was ultimately unsuccessful. After the Trail of Tears transplanted the Cherokee across the Mississippi River, Ross helped write a constitution for the Cherokee Nation.
oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:source: Coile, Grace Armstrong Collection of Robert Armstrong Papers 1790-1930 (THS Collection)

John Baldridge, Thomas Wilson, and Edward Gunter were Cherokee who received reservations from the United States government after the Treaty of 1819. They fought in the Creek War, including at the Battle of Horseshoe Bend. Wilson served under John Brown, while Baldridge served under Rain Crow. Edward Gunter was severely wounded during the battle. Guntersville, Alabama was formed around Edward Gunter's ferry described in this survey and named for him.

oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:title: Survey of division of Jonathan Ayres' land and slaves
oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:description: A hand-drawn survey of the division of Jonathan Ayres land on beaver creek. Lot No.1 (74 acres) went to Nancy Ayres along with two slaves, Wiley and Mary. Lot No. 1 is adjacent to John Coward's land. Lot No. 2 (84 acres) went to John Marley and Betsey Ayres along with two slaves, Fanny and Matilda. Lot No. 3 (73 acres) went to Joseph Ayres along with two slaves, Americus and George. Lot No. 4 (68 acres) went to Daniel McCollum and Polly Ayres along with two slaves, Eliza and Lucinda. oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:description: Two copies of a photolithograph, dated April 17, 1906, of an 1834 Mississippi land survey. The map is gridlined and subdivided into 36 sections, each of which represents approximately one square mile. Copy 2 of the map contains a section in the bottom-left quadrant that has been shaded in red and labelled "#4".

In 1830, the Choctaw Nation and the US Government signed the Treaty of Dancing Rabbit Creek, which was the first treaty made under the Indian Removal Act. The Choctaw agreed to forfeit all of their remaining land in the state of Mississippi in exchange for land in the Oklahoma Territory. Under the terms of the treaty, the Choctaw who removed to Oklahoma would retain their sovereign status, while those who stayed in Mississippi could become US citizens and be granted 640 acres of land.

oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:title: Spottsylvania Court House
oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:description: Detailed map of Spottsylvania showing roads, railroads, landowners names, and the location of the court house. Troop positions are shown with Union forces in blue and Confederate forces in red. Surveyed and drawn by Major J.E. Weyss, assisted by F. Theilkuhl, J. Strasser and G. Thompson.

The Battle of Spotsylvania Court House, part of Union Lieutenant General Ulysses S. Grant's Overland Campaign, was fought in May 1864. The court house served as a critical landmark with Confederate General Robert E. Lee's army pushing Union armies back to the court house and engaging in more trench warfare. Multiple attempts on both sides, including hand-to-hand combat, resulted in little progress and an eventual stalemate. Even though it was an indecisive battle, it became one of the deadliest campaigns of the Civil War, with more than 30,000 casualties.

The United States Coast Survey can trace its roots to an act signed into law by President Thomas Jefferson in 1807 to generate maritime charts for the newly formed nation. Ferdinand Hassler was selected as the first superintendent in 1816 and served until the jurisdiction of the survey was moved under the control of the Army in 1818. He was reappointed superintendent by President Andrew Jackson in 1832 with the department once again under civilian control. The Coast Survey created nautical charts, performed hydrographic surveys, as well as executed the first studies of the Gulf Stream. Known as the United States Coast and Geodetic Survey beginning in 1878, the department provided much needed work for engineers during the Great Depression and helped create maps and charts for the Allies in World War II. In 1970, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration was formed and was given control over the agency.

The United States Coast Survey can trace its roots to an act signed into law by President Thomas Jefferson in 1807 to generate maritime charts for the newly formed nation. Ferdinand Hassler was selected as the first superintendent in 1816 and served until the jurisdiction of the survey was moved under the control of the Army in 1818. He was reappointed superintendent by President Andrew Jackson in 1832 with the department once again under civilian control. The Coast Survey created nautical charts, performed hydrographic surveys, as well as executed the first studies of the Gulf Stream. Known as the United States Coast and Geodetic Survey beginning in 1878, the department provided much needed work for engineers during the Great Depression and helped create maps and charts for the Allies in World War II. In 1970, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration was formed and was given control over the agency.

oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:description: Coastal survey showing Salem Harbor and the adjacent part of Massachusetts Bay. The towns of Salem, Beverley, and Marblehead are shown along with every house structure. Includes sailing information and 2 coastal panoramas. Relief shown by hachures. Depths shown by contours and soundings.

The United States Coast Survey can trace its roots to an act signed into law by President Thomas Jefferson in 1807 to generate maritime charts for the newly formed nation. Ferdinand Hassler was selected as the first superintendent in 1816 and served until the jurisdiction of the survey was moved under the control of the Army in 1818. He was reappointed superintendent by President Andrew Jackson in 1832 with the department once again under civilian control. The Coast Survey created nautical charts, performed hydrographic surveys, as well as executed the first studies of the Gulf Stream. Known as the United States Coast and Geodetic Survey beginning in 1878, the department provided much needed work for engineers during the Great Depression and helped create maps and charts for the Allies in World War II. In 1970, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration was formed and was given control over the agency.

Also shows the Richmond and Petersburg Railroad, the Richmond and Danville Railroad, the York River Railroad, the James River, landowners names, roads, and topography. Surveyed and drawn by Major J.E. Weyss, assisted by F. Theilkuhl, J. Strasser, and G. Thompson.

Richmond (Va.) served as the Confederate capital during the Civil War. Because of this, it became the target of numerous attempts by the Union Army to overtake the city, notably during the Peninsula Campaign of 1862 and the Overland Campaign of 1864. The city finally fell on April 2, 1865.

The United States Coast Survey can trace its roots to an act signed into law by President Thomas Jefferson in 1807 to generate maritime charts for the newly formed nation. Ferdinand Hassler was selected as the first superintendent in 1816 and served until the jurisdiction of the survey was moved under the control of the Army in 1818. He was reappointed superintendent by President Andrew Jackson in 1832 with the department once again under civilian control. The Coast Survey created nautical charts, performed hydrographic surveys, as well as executed the first studies of the Gulf Stream. Known as the United States Coast and Geodetic Survey beginning in 1878, the department provided much needed work for engineers during the Great Depression and helped create maps and charts for the Allies in World War II. In 1970, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration was formed and was given control over the agency.

The United States Coast Survey can trace its roots to an act signed into law by President Thomas Jefferson in 1807 to generate maritime charts for the newly formed nation. Ferdinand Hassler was selected as the first superintendent in 1816 and served until the jurisdiction of the survey was moved under the control of the Army in 1818. He was reappointed superintendent by President Andrew Jackson in 1832 with the department once again under civilian control. The Coast Survey created nautical charts, performed hydrographic surveys, as well as executed the first studies of the Gulf Stream. Known as the United States Coast and Geodetic Survey beginning in 1878, the department provided much needed work for engineers during the Great Depression and helped create maps and charts for the Allies in World War II. In 1970, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration was formed and was given control over the agency.

Ferdinand Hassler was selected as the first superintendent in 1816 and served until the jurisdiction of the survey was moved under the control of the Army in 1818. He was reappointed superintendent by President Andrew Jackson in 1832 with the department once again under civilian control. The Coast Survey created nautical charts, performed hydrographic surveys, as well as executed the first studies of the Gulf Stream. Known as the United States Coast and Geodetic Survey beginning in 1878, the department provided much needed work for engineers during the Great Depression and helped create maps and charts for the Allies in World War II. In 1970, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration was formed and was given control over the agency.

oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:title: Pre-Revolutionary war-era map of the North Carolina, South Carolin and Virginia
oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:description: This hand-drawn map depicts the Old Southwest frontier, possibly around 1756, according to a pencilled inscription. The boundary between Virginia and North Carolina is drawn, as is the trans-Mississippi River ""Bounds of Virginia & New England"" and a rudamentary depiction of Georgia. The map details many French and English forts as well as the location of Native American tribes and settlements across the region. Shows Earl Granville's property in North Carolina.

Though the provenance of this map is unclear, it does belong to some of the earliest papers collected by the Tennessee Historical Society or its predecessor, the Tennessee Antiquarian Society. It may have been drawn by one of the surviving Cumberland settlers, since it uses very dated mid-18th century place-names and French colonial spellings for a number of sites.

oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:title: Preliminary movements, September 18th, 1863 : Map of the battlefield of Chickamauga
oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:description: Plate II of the Atlas of the battlefields of Chickamauga, Chattanooga, and vicinity. Topographical map of battlefield showing positions and names of opposing units at the time depicted.

The Battle of Chickamauga (September 19-20, 1863) was the most prominent Confederate victory in the Western Theater of the Civil War, and was the stage for the second most casualties sustained in the war after Gettysburg. Union Major General William Rosecrans' Army of the Cumberland (~60,000 men) was commanded to take Chattanooga, after a successful Tullahoma Campaign. They crossed the Tennessee River on August 16, and marched southeast. The Confederate Army of Tennessee (~65,000 men), commanded by General Braxton Bragg, retreated from Chattanooga on September 8, toward Lafayette, Georgia, and the Union captured the city the following day. The two forces finally met at West Chickamauga Creek, Georgia, on September 19. A day of fierce fighting saw only a little ground gained by the Confederates primarily in the middle by Generals Benjamin Cheatham, A. P. Stewart, and Bushrod Johnson, and the right flank by Walker and Forrest. September 20th began with another Confederate assault on the Union left, led by General Leonidas Polk. The attack waned by noon. A miscommunication between General Rosecrans and Brigadier General Thomas Wood saw Wood's brigade leave a hole in the line to support Brig. General John Brannan. General Longstreet took advantage and sent a three-division column let by General John Bell Hood to attack the weakened center. The assault rattled the Union troops who retreated to Horseshoe Ridge, where they were able to hold out the rest of the evening. Most were able to retreat to Chattanooga, but the three regiments left to cover the retreat were captured. The battle resulted in 16,710 casualties for the Union, and 18,454 for the Confederates. It is seen as a Confederate victory but the number of casualties left it a qualified one.

oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:title: Post route map of the states of Kentucky and Tennessee showing post offices with the intermediate distances and mail routes in operation on the 1st of December 1899
oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:description: Map showing the postal routes throughout Kentucky and Tennessee in 1899. A key under the title explains how often the mail service routes delivered from six times a week to special supply only. There are 96 counties listed in Tennessee, due to James County being included. Rivers and creeks are illustrated as are major railroads. Negative photocopy.

Established in 1871, James County existed for 48 years until a referendum dissolved it in 1920. Predominately white, rural, and poor, James County arose out of the political factionalism of the Reconstruction Era. In 1871, Representative Elbert A. James, a Democrat from Hamilton County, introduced legislation for the formation of the county, named in honor of his father, Rev. Jesse J. James. Lawmakers chose Ooltewah as the county seat, and subsequently citizens began work on building a county courthouse. Following 19 years of meager existence, state lawmakers passed an act on March 11, 1890 abolishing the county and returning the land to the parent counties of Hamilton and Bradley.

oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:title: Polk County, Tennessee, 1840-1860
oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:description: Copy of a map that depicts Polk County in the mid-19th century. The Hiwassee, Ocoee, and Conasauga Rivers flow through the county. Ducktown, Isabella, Benton, Copperhill and various old houses, Indian towns, landings, ferries, and fords are included

Robert Edward Barclay was born in Ringgold, Georgia, in 1893. Barclay served in the AEF during World War I and was awarded the Silver Star and Croix de Guerre. In the 1920s, Barclay worked for the Tennessee Copper Company in Copperhill, Tennessee. He researched and wrote a book about Ducktown and an early mining entrepreneur, Julius Raht, titled Ducktown - Back in Raht's Time. For the remainder of his life, Barclay served on many boards, commissions, and historical associations and authored two more books on mining in southeastern Tennessee. He died 1981.

The United States Coast Survey can trace its roots to an act signed into law by President Thomas Jefferson in 1807 to generate maritime charts for the newly formed nation. Ferdinand Hassler was selected as the first superintendent in 1816 and served until the jurisdiction of the survey was moved under the control of the Army in 1818. He was reappointed superintendent by President Andrew Jackson in 1832 with the department once again under civilian control. The Coast Survey created nautical charts, performed hydrographic surveys, as well as executed the first studies of the Gulf Stream. Known as the United States Coast and Geodetic Survey beginning in 1878, the department provided much needed work for engineers during the Great Depression and helped create maps and charts for the Allies in World War II. In 1970, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration was formed and was given control over the agency.

Robert Edward Barclay was born in Ringgold, Georgia, in 1893. Barclay served in the AEF during World War I and was awarded the Silver Star and Croix de Guerre. In the 1920s, Barclay worked for the Tennessee Copper Company in Copperhill, Tennessee. He researched and wrote a book about Ducktown and an early mining entrepreneur, Julius Raht, titled Ducktown - Back in Raht's Time. For the remainder of his life, Barclay served on many boards, commissions, and historical associations and authored two more books on mining in southeastern Tennessee. He died 1981.

North Anna

Troop positions are shown with Union forces in blue and Confederate forces in red. Surveyed and drawn by Major J.E. Weyss, assisted by F. Theilkuhl, J. Strasser and G. Thompson.

The Battle of North Anna was fought in May 1864 near the North Anna River between the armies of Union Lieutenant General Ulysses S. Grant and Confederate General Robert E. Lee. Lee attempted to create a "V" of defensive earthworks (ditches and trenches) to split the Union advances. The plan fell through, however, and both sides ended in a stalemate with Grant eventually moving his troops south.

The United States Coast Survey can trace its roots to an act signed into law by President Thomas Jefferson in 1807 to generate maritime charts for the newly formed nation. Ferdinand Hassler was selected as the first superintendent in 1816 and served until the jurisdiction of the survey was moved under the control of the Army in 1818. He was reappointed superintendent by President Andrew Jackson in 1832 with the department once again under civilian control. The Coast Survey created nautical charts, performed hydrographic surveys, as well as executed the first studies of the Gulf Stream. Known as the United States Coast and Geodetic Survey beginning in 1878, the department provided much needed work for engineers during the Great Depression and helped create maps and charts for the Allies in World War II. In 1970, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration was formed and was given control over the agency.

oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:title: Movements and positions preceding Battle of Chickamauga
oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:description: Shows campaign area preceding the battle of Chickamauga of June and July 1863. It outlines troop movements, battle lines and geographic details such as rivers, mountains, creeks, and ridges. Labeled as No. 8.

The Battle of Chickamauga (September 19-20, 1863) was the most prominent Confederate victory in the Western Theater of the Civil War, and was the stage for the second most casualties sustained in the war after Gettysburg. Union Major General William Rosecrans' Army of the Cumberland (~60,000 men) was commanded to take Chattanooga, after a successful Tullahoma Campaign. They crossed the Tennessee River on August 16, and marched southeast. The Confederate Army of Tennessee (~65,000 men), commanded by General Braxton Bragg, retreated from Chattanooga on September 8, toward Lafayette, Georgia, and the Union captured the city the following day. The two forces finally met at West Chickamauga Creek, Georgia, on September 19. A day of fierce fighting saw only a little ground gained by the Confederates primarily in the middle by Generals Benjamin Cheatham, A. P. Stewart, and Bushrod Johnson, and the right flank by Walker and Forrest. September 20th began with another Confederate assault on the Union left, led by General Leonidas Polk. The attack waned by noon. A miscommunication between General Rosecrans and Brigadier General Thomas Wood saw Wood's brigade leave a hole in the line to support Brig. General John Brannan. General Longstreet took advantage and sent a three-division column let by General John Bell Hood to attack the weakened center. The assault rattled the Union troops who retreated to Horseshoe Ridge, where they were able to hold out the rest of the evening. Most were able to retreat to Chattanooga, but the three regiments left to cover the retreat were captured. The battle resulted in 16,710 casualties for the Union, and 18,454 for the Confederates. It is seen as a Confederate victory but the number of casualties left it a qualified one.

The United States Coast Survey can trace its roots to an act signed into law by President Thomas Jefferson in 1807 to generate maritime charts for the newly formed nation. Ferdinand Hassler was selected as the first superintendent in 1816 and served until the jurisdiction of the survey was moved under the control of the Army in 1818. He was reappointed superintendent by President Andrew Jackson in 1832 with the department once again under civilian control. The Coast Survey created nautical charts, performed hydrographic surveys, as well as executed the first studies of the Gulf Stream. Known as the United States Coast and Geodetic Survey beginning in 1878, the department provided much needed work for engineers during the Great Depression and helped create maps and charts for the Allies in World War II. In 1970, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration was formed and was given control over the agency.

Robert Edward Barclay was born in Ringgold, Georgia, in 1893. Barclay served in the AEF during World War I and was awarded the Silver Star and Croix de Guerre. In the 1920s, Barclay worked for the Tennessee Copper Company in Copperhill, Tennessee. He researched and wrote a book about Ducktown and an early mining entrepreneur, Julius Raht, titled Ducktown - Back in Raht's Time. For the remainder of his life, Barclay served on many boards, commissions, and historical associations and authored two more books on mining in southeastern Tennessee. He died 1981.
