oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:title: Mare Island Straits, California
oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:description: Coastal survey showing the Mare Island Straits off the coast of California. Oriented with north toward upper left. Relief shown by hachures and depths shown by soundings and isolines. Also shows Mare Island, Carquinez Straits and site of Vallejo.

The United States Coast Survey can trace its roots to an act signed into law by President Thomas Jefferson in 1807 to generate maritime charts for the newly formed nation. Ferdinand Hassler was selected as the first superintendent in 1816 and served until the jurisdiction of the survey was moved under the control of the Army in 1818. He was reappointed superintendent by President Andrew Jackson in 1832 with the department once again under civilian control. The Coast Survey created nautical charts, performed hydrographic surveys, as well as executed the first studies of the Gulf Stream. Known as the United States Coast and Geodetic Survey beginning in 1878, the department provided much needed work for engineers during the Great Depression and helped create maps and charts for the Allies in World War II. In 1970, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration was formed and was given control over the agency.

oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:title: Map of the city of Nashville Davidson County Tennessee 1908
oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:description: Detailed color map of Nashville, Tennessee from 1908 showing street names, city ward boundaries, railroads, cemeteries and other landmarks. Streetcar lines are marked in red. A directory is on the right side. On bottom in red ink: ""Compliments of Lytton Taylor candidate for county judge. Subject to Democratic primary, Thursday, December 9, 1909.""

Griffith Morgan Hopkins was born around 1836, however the exact date is unknown. He first began printing maps in 1857 and continued until his retirement in 1900. He founded G. M. Hopkins & Co. with his brother Henry W. Hopkins, and together they produced many city and county atlases, primarily of the northeast, from their shop in Philadelphia. Their 1908 Atlas of Nashville is a fine, block-by-block depiction of the town in a period of growth to a modern urban center. G. M. Hopkins & Co. continued on after the founders' retirements until the Great Depression ended the demand for their atlases. The company was sold to the Franklin Survey Company in 1943, with the name intact, due to its association with quality.

oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:title: Map of the Battlefield of Antietam, Sept. 17th - Noon to 12:15 PM
oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:description: Originally from the Atlas of the battlefield of Antietam, this map shows the movements of the Confederate Reserve Artillery battalions and Union divisions of the Fourth Corps and Fifth Corps in the early afternoon of Sept. 17, 1862.

The Confederate Reserve Artillery battalions of Col. J. Thompson Brown and Maj. William Nelson crossed to the Virginia side of the Potomac on the morning of September 15th. Brown's battalion was put in position to guard the ford. Nelson's battalion went down the river and took position on the heights commanding Blackford's ford. At daybreak Couch's Division, Fourth Corps, marched from Crampton's Gap down Pleasant Valley to occupy Maryland Heights. When near the foot of the Valley its orders were countermanded and the division reached the field late in the evening of the 17th. On the morning of the 17th, Humphrey's Division, Fifth Corps, was near Frederick. At 3:30 P.M., it marched for Sharpsburg and reached the field early in the morning of the 18th.
oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:creator: United States. War Department

oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:description: Portion of Geological map of state of Tennessee (1855) (Map 3011) showing the upper right including copper mines located in southeastern Tennessee.

Robert Edward Barclay was born in Ringgold, Georgia, in 1893. Barclay served in the AEF during World War I and was awarded the Silver Star and Croix de Guerre. In the 1920s, Barclay worked for the Tennessee Copper Company in Copperhill, Tennessee. He researched and wrote a book about Ducktown and an early mining entrepreneur, Julius Raht, titled Ducktown - Back in Raht's Time. For the remainder of his life, Barclay served on many boards, commissions, and historical associations and authored two more books on mining in southeastern Tennessee. He died 1981.

Charles Alfred Proctor, a civil engineer, helped found the Hibernia Mining Company in 1856 to extract, work, smelt, and manufacture copper in southeastern Tennessee. He also established the Citico Mining Company, Clinch Coal Company, Athena Coal Company, and Caledonia Iron Company. In 1852, Proctor was among the founding trustees of Eureka College, a Methodist Episcopal Church, South school in Monroe County.

The United States Coast Survey can trace its roots to an act signed into law by President Thomas Jefferson in 1807 to generate maritime charts for the newly formed nation. Ferdinand Hassler was selected as the first superintendent in 1816 and served until the jurisdiction of the survey was moved under the control of the Army in 1818. He was reappointed superintendent by President Andrew Jackson in 1832 with the department once again under civilian control. The Coast Survey created nautical charts, performed hydrographic surveys, as well as executed the first studies of the Gulf Stream. Known as the United States Coast and Geodetic Survey beginning in 1878, the department provided much needed work for engineers during the Great Depression and helped create maps and charts for the Allies in World War II. In 1970, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration was formed and was given control over the agency.

Robert Edward Barclay was born in Ringgold, Georgia, in 1893. Barclay served in the AEF during World War I and was awarded the Silver Star and Croix de Guerre. In the 1920s, Barclay worked for the Tennessee Copper Company in Copperhill, Tennessee. He researched and wrote a book about Ducktown and an early mining entrepreneur, Julius Raht, titled Ducktown - Back in Raht's Time. For the remainder of his life, Barclay served on many boards, commissions, and historical associations and authored two more books on mining in southeastern Tennessee. He died 1981.

The United States Coast Survey can trace its roots to an act signed into law by President Thomas Jefferson in 1807 to generate maritime charts for the newly formed nation. Ferdinand Hassler was selected as the first superintendent in 1816 and served until the jurisdiction of the survey was moved under the control of the Army in 1818. He was reappointed superintendent by President Andrew Jackson in 1832 with the department once again under civilian control. The Coast Survey created nautical charts, performed hydrographic surveys, as well as executed the first studies of the Gulf Stream. Known as the United States Coast and Geodetic Survey beginning in 1878, the department provided much needed work for engineers during the Great Depression and helped create maps and charts for the Allies in World War II. In 1970, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration was formed and was given control over the agency.

oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:title: Fredericksburg
oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:description: Detailed map of the environs of Fredericksburg giving Confederate entrenchments in red. Also shows the Richmond, Fredericksburg and Potomac Rail Road, landowners names, roads, and topography. Surveyed and drawn by Major J.E. Weyss, assisted by F. Theilkuhl, J. Strasser and G. Thompson.

The Battle of Fredericksburg was fought in December 1862 in Fredericksburg, Virginia, between Confederate General Robert E. Lee's Army of Northern Virginia and Union Major General Ambrose Burnside's Army of the Potomac. Burnside ordered his men to assault the entrenched Confederate line. Successive charges failed until Burnside asked Lee for a truce on December 14. On December 15 Federal forces withdrew across the Rappahannock River. The Union suffered 12,653 casualties, while the Confederates sustained only 4,201.

oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:title: Map of Chickamauga Park
oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:description: Plate XIV of the Atlas of the battlefields of Chickamauga, Chattanooga, and vicinity. Topographical map shows the park boundaries, churhces, roads and battlefield stations.

The Battle of Chickamauga (September 19-20, 1863) was the most prominent Confederate victory in the Western Theater of the Civil War, and was the stage for the second most casualties sustained in the war after Gettysburg. Union Major General William Rosecrans' Army of the Cumberland (~60,000 men) was commanded to take Chattanooga, after a successful Tullahoma Campaign. They crossed the Tennessee River on August 16, and marched southeast. The Confederate Army of Tennessee (~65,000 men), commanded by General Braxton Bragg, retreated from Chattanooga on September 8, toward Lafayette, Georgia, and the Union captured the city the following day. The two forces finally met at West Chickamauga Creek, Georgia, on September 19. A day of fierce fighting saw only a little ground gained by the Confederates primarily in the middle by Generals Benjamin Cheatham, A. P. Stewart, and Bushrod Johnson, and the right flank by Walker and Forrest. September 20th began with another Confederate assault on the Union left, led by General Leonidas Polk. The attack waned by noon. A miscommunication between General Rosecrans and Brigadier General Thomas Wood saw Wood's brigade leave a hole in the line to support Brig. General John Brannan. General Longstreet took advantage and sent a three-division column let by General John Bell Hood to attack the weakened center. The assault rattled the Union troops who retreated to Horseshoe Ridge, where they were able to hold out the rest of the evening. Most were able to retreat to Chattanooga, but the three regiments left to cover the retreat were captured. The battle resulted in 16,710 casualties for the Union, and 18,454 for the Confederates. It is seen as a Confederate victory but the number of casualties left it a qualified one.

The United States Coast Survey can trace its roots to an act signed into law by President Thomas Jefferson in 1807 to generate maritime charts for the newly formed nation. Ferdinand Hassler was selected as the first superintendent in 1816 and served until the jurisdiction of the survey was moved under the control of the Army in 1818. He was reappointed superintendent by President Andrew Jackson in 1832 with the department once again under civilian control. The Coast Survey created nautical charts, performed hydrographic surveys, as well as executed the first studies of the Gulf Stream. Known as the United States Coast and Geodetic Survey beginning in 1878, the department provided much needed work for engineers during the Great Depression and helped create maps and charts for the Allies in World War II. In 1970, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration was formed and was given control over the agency.

oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:description: Map showing hydrographic details of Key West Harbor in Florida. Includes notes on currents, tides sailing directions, abbreviation table, 4 views and 1 inset map "Sub-sketch of Key West harbor"

The United States Coast Survey can trace its roots to an act signed into law by President Thomas Jefferson in 1807 to generate maritime charts for the newly formed nation. Ferdinand Hassler was selected as the first superintendent in 1816 and served until the jurisdiction of the survey was moved under the control of the Army in 1818. He was reappointed superintendent by President Andrew Jackson in 1832 with the department once again under civilian control. The Coast Survey created nautical charts, performed hydrographic surveys, as well as executed the first studies of the Gulf Stream. Known as the United States Coast and Geodetic Survey beginning in 1878, the department provided much needed work for engineers during the Great Depression and helped create maps and charts for the Allies in World War II. In 1970, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration was formed and was given control over the agency.

Robert E. Lee retreated through Farmville with his army to escape Union forces. The Confederate Army planned to use Farmville as a place to get rations to feed its soldiers. General Robert E. Robert Edward Barclay was born in Ringgold, Georgia, in 1893. Barclay served in the AEF during World War I and was awarded the Silver Star and Croix de Guerre. In the 1920s, Barclay worked for the Tennessee Copper Company in Copperhill, Tennessee. He researched and wrote a book about Ducktown and an early mining entrepreneur, Julius Raht, titled Ducktown - Back in Raht's Time. For the remainder of his life, Barclay served on many boards, commissions, and historical associations and authored two more books on mining in southeastern Tennessee. He died 1981.

The United States Coast Survey can trace its roots to an act signed into law by President Thomas Jefferson in 1807 to generate maritime charts for the newly formed nation. Ferdinand Hassler was selected as the first superintendent in 1816 and served until the jurisdiction of the survey was moved under the control of the Army in 1818. He was reappointed superintendent by President Andrew Jackson in 1832 with the department once again under civilian control. The Coast Survey created nautical charts, performed hydrographic surveys, as well as executed the first studies of the Gulf Stream. Known as the United States Coast and Geodetic Survey beginning in 1878, the department provided much needed work for engineers during the Great Depression and helped create maps and charts for the Allies in World War II. In 1970, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration was formed and was given control over the agency.

The Battle of Harpers Ferry was fought in September 1862 in current-day West Virginia between Thomas "Stonewall" Jackson's Confederate Army and Colonel Dixon Mile's garrison. Jackson surrounded the town and relentlessly shelled the garrison until Miles surrendered. The Confederates captured 12,000 men, 13,000 small arms, 200 wagons, and 73 artillery pieces from the Harpers Ferry Armory.

The United States Coast Survey can trace its roots to an act signed into law by President Thomas Jefferson in 1807 to generate maritime charts for the newly formed nation. Ferdinand Hassler was selected as the first superintendent in 1816 and served until the jurisdiction of the survey was moved under the control of the Army in 1818. He was reappointed superintendent by President Andrew Jackson in 1832 with the department once again under civilian control. The Coast Survey created nautical charts, performed hydrographic surveys, as well as executed the first studies of the Gulf Stream. Known as the United States Coast and Geodetic Survey beginning in 1878, the department provided much needed work for engineers during the Great Depression and helped create maps and charts for the Allies in World War II. In 1970, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration was formed and was given control over the agency.

oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:title: Geological map of Sevier County, Tenn.
oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:description: Drawn by Gerard Troost, Tennessee's first State Geologist, this geological map of Sevier County shows rivers, the Great Smoky Mountains and mineral resources including slate and limestone. Other landmarks include the Holston River, the towns of Dandrige and Sevierville, Yellow Springs, Wiers Cove and Dawson's Cove.

This map was printed in the Sixth Report (to the Tennessee General Assembly) of Dr. Gerard Troost, State Geologist. Troost, a native of the Netherlands, was Tennessee's first state geologist and first president of the Philadelphia Academy of Natural Sciences. He served as professor of chemistry, geology, and mineralogy at the University of Nashville for 22 years. For more information on Troost, consult the article in the Peabody Journal of Education 30, no. 5 (March 1953) by Ellen V. Piers, called "Girard Troost, Pioneer Scientist" pages 265-274.

The United States Coast Survey can trace its roots to an act signed into law by President Thomas Jefferson in 1807 to generate maritime charts for the newly formed nation. Ferdinand Hassler was selected as the first superintendent in 1816 and served until the jurisdiction of the survey was moved under the control of the Army in 1818. He was reappointed superintendent by President Andrew Jackson in 1832 with the department once again under civilian control. The Coast Survey created nautical charts, performed hydrographic surveys, as well as executed the first studies of the Gulf Stream. Known as the United States Coast and Geodetic Survey beginning in 1878, the department provided much needed work for engineers during the Great Depression and helped create maps and charts for the Allies in World War II. In 1970, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration was formed and was given control over the agency.

Samuel Anderson Weakley was a chief in the operation division of the U.S. Corps of Engineers in Nashville, Tenn. as well as a genealogist. He did careful deed research to produce his plats of early North Carolina land grants, which can be found in TSLA's collection of his papers. He assembled the greater part of his research into a book, "The Southern Virginia Weakley Families and Their Descendents" also available at the Library & Archives.

oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:description: Map detailing the environs of Cold Harbor (Va.) with Confederate movements in red and Union movements in blue. Also shows the Virginia Central Railroad, the Chickahominy River, roads, names of residences, mills, and topography. Surveyed and drawn by Major J.E. Weyss, assisted by F. Theilkuhl, J. Strasser, and G. Thompson.

The Battle of Cold Harbor was fought from May 31 to June 12, 1864 at Cold Harbor in Hanover County (Va." Considered one of the most lopsided engagements of the Civil War, Confederate General Robert E. Lee gained a defensive victory when he and his army had time to establish approximately 7 miles of entrenchment to repulse Union Major General Ulysses S. Grant's army, suffering almost five times the casualties of the Union.

oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:title: City of San Francisco and its vicinity, California
oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:description: Coastal survey showing San Francisco and its vicinity. Public buildings are illustrated including city hall, churches, hospitals, post offices and offices. Also shows streets, reservoirs, Mission Bay and Mission de Dolores. The outlines and topography are engraved by Max. F. O. Strobel with lettering by E. F. Woodward. Relief shown by contours and depths shown by soundings.

The United States Coast Survey can trace its roots to an act signed into law by President Thomas Jefferson in 1807 to generate maritime charts for the newly formed nation. Ferdinand Hassler was selected as the first superintendent in 1816 and served until the jurisdiction of the survey was moved under the control of the Army in 1818. He was reappointed superintendent by President Andrew Jackson in 1832 with the department once again under civilian control. The Coast Survey created nautical charts, performed hydrographic surveys, as well as executed the first studies of the Gulf Stream. Known as the United States Coast and Geodetic Survey beginning in 1878, the department provided much needed work for engineers during the Great Depression and helped create maps and charts for the Allies in World War II. In 1970, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration was formed and was given control over the agency.

In 1830, the Choctaw Nation and the U.S. Government signed the Treaty of Dancing Rabbit Creek, which was the first treaty made under the Indian Removal Act. The Choctaw agreed to forfeit all of their remaining land in the state of Mississippi in exchange for land in the Oklahoma Territory. Under the terms of the treaty, the Choctaw who removed to Oklahoma would retain their sovereign status, while those who stayed in Mississippi could become U.S. citizens and be granted 640 acres of land.

In 1830, the Choctaw Nation and the U.S. Government signed the Treaty of Dancing Rabbit Creek, which was the first treaty made under the Indian Removal Act. The Choctaw agreed to forfeit all of their remaining land in the state of Mississippi in exchange for land in the Oklahoma Territory. Under the terms of the treaty, the Choctaw who removed to Oklahoma would retain their sovereign status, while those who stayed in Mississippi could become U.S. citizens and be granted 640 acres of land. oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:description: This colorful map shows the different routes of the Nashville, Chattanooga and St. Louis railway and how it reached different communities in Tennessee. Includes pamphlet. Pamphlet describes land for sale in various counties contiguous to the railroad line.

During the 1870s - 1900s, America and Tennessee experienced a boom in railroads. Railroads offered a reliable and weatherproof means of transportation for the shipping of goods from one place to another. In Tennessee, the most prominent railroads that formed were the Louisville and Nashville Railroad (L & N) and the Nashville, Chattanooga & St. Louis Railroad (N.C. & St. L." As a result of the development of railroads, Tennessee cities grew into shipping and manufacturing centers. The United States Coast Survey can trace its roots to an act signed into law by President Thomas Jefferson in 1807 to generate maritime charts for the newly formed nation. Ferdinand Hassler was selected as the first superintendent in 1816 and served until the jurisdiction of the survey was moved under the control of the Army in 1818. He was reappointed superintendent by President Andrew Jackson in 1832 with the department once again under civilian control. The Coast Survey created nautical charts, performed hydrographic surveys, as well as executed the first studies of the Gulf Stream. Known as the United States Coast and Geodetic Survey beginning in 1878, the department provided much needed work for engineers during the Great Depression and helped create maps and charts for the Allies in World War II. In 1970, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration was formed and was given control over the agency.

British Lt. Henry Timberlake traveled to the Overhill Cherokee villages on the Little Tennessee river in late 1761 to explain the treaty signed at Fort Loudon to the Cherokees located there. He remained with the Cherokee until March 1762, keeping a journal that was published in 1765 and contains a detailed account of Cherokee life as well as this map. He later accompanied several Cherokee headmen, including Attakullakulla, the Little Carpenter, to London to meet with King George.

The Bermuda Hundred Campaign consisted of a series of battles fought in the small town outside of Richmond, Virginia. The five main battles fought during the campaign include: Port Walthall Junction, Swift Creek, Chester Station, Proctor's Creek, and Ware Bottom Church. Benjamin Franklin Cheatham was appointed brigadier general in the Confederate Army at the outbreak of the Civil War. The Battle of Appomattox Court House was the final engagement for Robert E. Lee's Army of Northern Virginia before their surrender there on April 9, 1865. Lee spent the week prior looking for provisions for his army, to no avail. On April 6, about 7,700 Confederates cut of from the main army were captured at Sailor's Creek. The following day, Grant suggested that Lee surrender the remainder of his army, but Lee refused. The two armies met at Appomattox Court House at dawn on April 9, the Union 150,000 strong, while only 28,000 remained of the Confederate Army of Northern Virginia. After a short skirmish and seeing that his army was overwhelmingly outnumbered, Lee agreed to surrender. The opposing generals met at the house of Wilmer McLean to discuss terms.

oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:title: A sketch of the Cherokee Country, being a reduced copy from Mante's History Engraved for Bancroft's History of the United States by G. G. Smith
oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:description: From George Bancroft's History of the United States, v. 4.

Thomas Mante was an English military writer who published a book entitled "The History of the Late War in North-America, and the islands of the West-Indies", in 1772. The map shows the relative location of the Lower, Middle, Valley, and Upper settlements of the Cherokee nation. All these settlements lay between Fort Loudon on the west and Fort Prince George, the colonial fort nearest to Fort Loudon, on the east. It illustrates just how isolated and far from help Fort Loudon was. Mante's map also illustrates the proximity of the headwaters of the Little Tennessee and the Savanna rivers, which both arise in an area the map identifies as "Herbert's Savana." English colonial leaders feared that the two waterways might provide a strategic route for French expeditions moving up the Tennessee and Little Tennessee rivers from French settlements on the Ohio and Mississippi rivers. Mante's map was subsequently adapted for publication in George Bancroft's History of the United States of America, from the Discovery of the American Continent to 1789. The ten volumes of Bancoft's History were published betwen 1834 and 1874. Americans of the time viewed Bancroft's work as the definitive account of the founding of our county.

oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:title: A mapp of Virginia discovered to ye hills and in it's latt: from 35. deg: & 1/2 neer Florida to 41. deg: bounds of new England
oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:description: A copy of this map originally drawn by John Farrer shows the eastern coast of North America from Cape Cod in present-day Massachusetts to Cape Fear in present-day North Carolina. Virginia is shown as on the route to the Sea of China and the East Indies. Other elements include a compass rose and scale. There are decorative drawings throughout the map including birds, sea monsters, a sea creature blowing a horn, a deer, a rabbit, a bear, and other animals.

Farrer was a prominent member of the Royal Company of Virginia explored much of Virginia searching for a route to the Pacific Ocean for the silk industry. Farrer's map is significant due to the narrow depiction of North America with a Northwest Passage shown as a river connecting the Hudson River to the Sea of China and the Indies. This copy came from the Maryland Geological Society's Winsor's Narrative and Critical History.
oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:creator: Farrer, John, 1590?-1657

oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:title: A chart exhibiting the normal course & velocity of the tidal current at ebb in Boston Harbor
oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:description: The United States Coast Survey can trace its roots to an act signed into law by President Thomas Jefferson in 1807 to generate maritime charts for the newly formed nation. Ferdinand Hassler was selected as the first superintendent in 1816 and served until the jurisdiction of the survey was moved under the control of the Army in 1818. He was reappointed superintendent by President Andrew Jackson in 1832 with the department once again under civilian control. The Coast Survey created nautical charts, performed hydrographic surveys, as well as executed the first studies of the Gulf Stream. Known as the United States Coast and Geodetic Survey beginning in 1878, the department provided much needed work for engineers during the Great Depression and helped create maps and charts for the Allies in World War II. In 1970, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration was formed and was given control over the agency.
oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:creator: United States Coast Survey

The United States Coast Survey can trace its roots to an act signed into law by President Thomas Jefferson in 1807 to generate maritime charts for the newly formed nation. Ferdinand Hassler was selected as the first superintendent in 1816 and served until the jurisdiction of the survey was moved under the control of the Army in 1818. He was reappointed superintendent by President Andrew Jackson in 1832 with the department once again under civilian control. The Coast Survey created nautical charts, performed hydrographic surveys, as well as executed the first studies of the Gulf Stream. Known as the United States Coast and Geodetic Survey beginning in 1878, the department provided much needed work for engineers during the Great Depression and helped create maps and charts for the Allies in World War II. In 1970, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration was formed and was given control over the agency.

Landowners map of Davidson County (approximately 1870)
oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:description: This extremely detailed hand-drawn map of Davidson County focuses on waterways and names land and property owners along them. The Edgefield and Kentucky Railroad can be seen running up through Madison Station (later called just Madison). Civil districts are labeled in pencil. Certain sections of the map were not inked and it appears the map was prepared in sections, with the top half having been turned upside down for easier access. Certain neighborhoods or towns are named, as well as tolls, mills, churches, and schools, including a "Colored Childrens School," located in the Hardscuffle community. The red lines represent roads, while the black lines represent waterways. This map is likely a draft by Davidson County surveyor Wilbur Foster or someone working under his supervision, as it mirrors closely--though not entirely--his 1871 published color map of the county. There are slight differences between the two maps in the data recorded.

This is one of the earliest maps of Davidson County that names property owners as well as various churches, public buildings and institutions. It is believed this may have been the precursor to Wilbur Foster's 1871 color map of Davidson County Tennessee (Map 2552), since the data and its placement match so closely to that map commissioned by the county court. The chief value of this map comes from the location of landowner's names, churches, and schools in post-Civil War Davidson County.

oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:title: Map of Jackson County, Tennessee showing civil districts (1836)
oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:description: Map of Jackson County from 1836 showing the first civil districts of the county. It shows a very detailed view of the waterways in the county, naming each river, creek, branch, and fork of the Cumberland River. Civil districts are drawn in faded red ink along with each district number. Each dotted line represents a road that serves as a district line, each are named as well, including the famous and important Walton Road. The center for holding elections in each district are represented as squares and denoted as "center." A legend is available in the bottom right and the scale is explained at the top. Written descriptions of the civil district boundaries are appended to the map.

These 1836 county maps showing the new civil districts, required by the new state constitution, written in 1834 and ratified the following year, which mandated such civil divisions for taxation purposes, were done for many counties. Jackson County was established by the Tennessee General Assembly in 1801 from part of Smith County and Native American lands. It is named for Andrew Jackson, at the time a Tennessee Supreme Court Justice and former U.S. Senator and Representative. Its county seat and largest city is Gainesboro, named for General Edmund Pendleton Gaines, a hero of the War of 1812.

Bradley County was established in 1836 from the Ocoee District of Cherokee territory. It is named for Revolutionary War and War of 1812 veteran, Colonel Edward Bradley. Its county seat and largest city is Cleveland, named for a commander at the Battle of King's Mountain, Colonel Benjamin Cleveland. Bradley County was one of the many East Tennessee counties that voted against secession during the outbreak of the Civil War.

oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:title: A new & accurate map of the provinces of North & South Carolina, Georgia.
oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:description: This 18th century map of the Southern colonies and their backcountry shows topographical features such as mountains, rivers, bays and inlets as well as forts, settlements, mines and towns. It is particularly noteworthy for its depiction of the native American landscape of the interior. Tennessee is shown as the "Country of the Cherokees." There is also a note on the Cherokees describing them as "a numerous & warlike nation...[who] serve as a powerful Barrier to Carolina & Georgia in ye present War against France & Spain," likely a reference to their alliance with Great Britain in King George's War with France and the War of Jenkins' Ear with Spain. Many Cherokee (and other Southern tribal) villages are shown. An "English Fort and Factory" is shown on the R[iver] Hogohegee (Tennessee River), and the Cumberland River is named the "Antient River of Chouanons" (Shawnee?" The Appalachian Mountains collectively are designated as the "Charokee Mountains."

Emanuel Bowen was an English map maker in the 18th century. He produced many well-known maps of the American colonies as well as county maps of England. His son was map maker Thomas Bowen. Two of his apprentices were renowned cartographers Thomas Kitchin and Thomas Jefferys. This map was no. 60 of 68 maps originally published in A Complete Atlas, or Distinct View of the Known World, and is a reprint from Bowen's earlier atlas: A Complete System of Geography, published in 1747. He served as geographer to King George II of England and Louis XV of France.

oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:title: Map of the various channels for conveying the trade of the north west to the Atlantic seaboard
oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:description: A map of the Eastern United States showing the various avenues of trade, including those affected by the enlargement of the Erie Canal. Canals are highlighted in green, the "present" drainage of the trade of the canal is highlighted in tan, while the drainage of trade after the enlargement of the canal is highlighted in red. Railroads, completed, in progress, and proposed, are denoted. The Great Lakes, major rivers affected by the Erie Canal, and important train stations are included.

The Erie Canal was undertaken in 1817 and completed in 1825, connecting the Great Lakes with the Hudson River, and thus the Atlantic Ocean. This map was created after one of the many enlargement projects aimed to increase traffic along the waterway. The Erie Canal is the most famous of the American canals and significantly lowered the cost of transporting goods between the north east and the midwest.

Peter S. Duval was born in France and trained as a lithographer in Paris. Fellow lithographer Cephas G. Childs met and hired Duval and brought him back to Philadelphia to work in his company. When Childs retired from the lithography business in 1834, he sold his interest in the firm to Duval and George Lehman. The company of Lehman & Duval moved the business to a building at Dock Street and Bank Alley in 1835. Lehman resigned in 1837, and the firm became known as P. S. Duval's Lithographic Establishment.

oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:title: Map of Maury County and part of Lewis, Lawrence and Giles (1851)
oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:description: This detailed map was originally from the Tennessee Supreme Court case of Maury County v. Lewis County. It shows a number of important historical and surveying landmarks as well as the boundaries of all the counties surrounding Lewis County. Depicted are the Natchez Trace, Meriwether Lewis' grave (for whom the county was named), and Grinder's Stand where he met his demise, the shared boundary of the old Military Reservation and Congressional Reservation, Gen. Range and section lines of the 7th and 8th Surveyor's Districts also shown.

oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:title: Linguistic stocks of American Indians north of Mexico
oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:description: From John Wesley Powell's Indian Linguistic Families of North America. This color map shows 58 areas of Indian habitation grouped by native language. The map is helpful in understanding the possible early relationships of the various Native American tribes, such as the linguistic affinities between the Cherokee and Iroquois Nations. Powell was one of the first American scientists to undertake ethnographic studies of native Americans, of which this map is an artifact. There is also a small inset of the Aleutian Islands in the lower left.

John Wesley Powell was the great Western explorer, geologist and Union veteran. Having lost his right arm at Shiloh, Powell went on to become the first director of the Smithsonian Bureau of Ethnology, the second director of the United States Geological Survey. He is credited with the first non-native exploration of the Grand Canyon and early efforts to preserve it and other natural wonders of the West. The map was compiled under the direction of Henry Gannett (1846-1914), who established the geography program in the U.S. Census Office. In 1882 he created a similar program at the USGS, which became the Division of Geography in 1885 and produced the first topographic map sheets published in the General Atlas of the United States four years later.

oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:title: Survey and plat of Thomas Molloy land on the Harpeth River (1801)
oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:description: Survey and plat of 640 acres of land in Williamson County, Tennessee owned and surveyed by Thomas Molloy. The land was originally assigned (sold) to Andrew Haddock, heir of Henry Hicks, by the State of North Carolina. 640 acres was the share granted by North Carolina to privates who had served in the Continental Army. Property is adjacent to land owned by James Robertson, which he purchased from Revolutionary War officer Capt. Peter B[e]cote. Molloy was, along with Robertson, among the earliest surveyors in Middle Tennessee; both were heavily involved in speculation in North Carolina military lands, of which this is an example. William McGah and John Hutton served as deputy surveyor Molloy's chain carriers.

Thomas Molloy was one of the earliest surveyors and settlers of Davidson County. Molloy's hand drawn plats are particularly fine examples of the early surveyors art in Tennessee. He was elected to the Inferior Court of Pleas for Davidson County in 1783 and was a prominent landowner in the area.

oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:description: Hand-drawn maps (one linen) of Rhea County, Tennessee show the civil districts laid out in 1836. It names rivers, creeks, certain roads, and county lines. Civil districts were also election precincts, and the map(s) show polling places--usually residences, but in one district a schoolhouse--where voting would take place within the district. Polling places include, in addition to the schoolhouse, Jones's, Whaley's, Hill's, Dyer's, Thompson's, and Paul's residences, and the city of Washington. Other important early locations in Rhea County are denoted, such as: Hornsby's Ferry, McKiddy's, Hoodenpyle's, Kelley's Ferry, West's Mill, Garwood's, and Mitchel's Spring.

These 1836 county maps showing the new civil districts, required by the new state constitution, written in 1834 and ratified the following year, which mandated such civil divisions for taxation purposes, were done for many counties. Rhea County was formed in 1807 from Roane County, and was split to form Meigs County in 1836. It is named for Revolutionary War veteran and Tennessee statesman, John Rhea. The county seat and largest city is Dayton, originally called Smith's Crossroads. It was renamed in 1877 after the city of Dayton, Ohio. Dayton was the stage for the famous Scopes Trial in 1925. Washington, shown on the map, was the most important city in Rhea County until the Cincinnati Southern Railway was laid out four miles west of it in 1880.

oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:description: Hand-drawn map of Wayne and Hardin counties, as well as parts of Perry, Hickman, and Henderson counties. Wayne and Hardin counties are divided into numbered ranges and sections. Map shows rivers, creeks, and river forks. It also identifies early towns in the area including: Hardin[s]ville, Savannah, Waynesboro, Lidden[s]ville (present-day Martins Mills), Carrollville (Clifton), Shan[n]onville, Lexington, and Perryville. Other features denoted are Huddleston Bluff and J. Rayburn's residence. The purpose of the map seems to be the division of land around the Tennessee River between the counties.

Wayne County was established in 1817 from portions of Hickman and Humphreys counties. It is named for Revolutionary War General Anthony Wayne. Its county seat is Waynesboro, and its largest city is Clifton, supposedly named because it is situated on a cliff. Hardin County was created in 1819 from land annexed in the Jackson Purchase. It is named for Revolutionary War veteran and early landowner, Joseph Hardin, Sr. Its county seat and largest city is Savannah, named for Savannah, Georgia.

oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:title: Knox County, Tennessee (approximately 1832)
oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:description: Hand-drawn map, possibly by Matthew Rhea, of Knox County (Tenn.) showing Knoxville, Clinton, Maryville, Sevierville, Gravesville, Loveville (Lovell), and Louisville. The Holston (Tennessee) and Clinch rivers and tributaries are depicted and labeled. Other geographic features such as Chestnut Ridge, Black Oak Ridge, Bull Run, and Copper Ridge are shown. These features are important for understanding early Knox County surveys, as they are some of the landmarks used. McBee's Ferry, Campbell's Station, and Meredith's are denoted. The Ramsey House, also known as Mecklenburg, is shown on the map, however it is written as McLinburg. Survey notes are listed on reverse.

This map, along with his other county maps, may have been used by Matthew Rhea in preparing his seminal 1834 map of the State of Tennessee with cousin Joseph Campbell Rhea. An important geographical feature of Knox County is the origin of the Tennessee River at the union of the Holston and French Broad rivers.

Engraver John M. Atwood was born in Washington, D.C. around 1818. Active in New York City from 1838 to 1852, he drew and engraved maps with Thomas A. Story for many American mapmakers, including the Colton Company, Humphrey Phelps, and Ensigns & Thayer. Humphrey Phelps was a publisher in New York City from the early 1830s until the 1850s, often working with Ensigns & Thayer, Thomas Fanning, and Gaylord Watson, producing maps, prints and books. Phelps is primarily known for travel guides, or foldable pocket maps, which he began producing in 1838. Timothy and Edward Ensign were lithographers, and map and book publishers in New York City. They formed the publishing firm Ensigns & Thayer with Horace Thayer, and worked together until Timothy's death in 1849. Edward continued with Ensigns & Thayer until about 1854, when he became a partner of Ensign, Bridgman & Fanning, another publishing firm.

This map appeared as an illustration for an article on a 1759 British-Cherokee treaty negotiation that was published in the March, 1760 issue of London Magazine. It depicts the location of the same Cherokee settlements shown on the Thomas Mante map, but with a more accurate geographic orientation. As a note on the map explains, it mistakenly identifies today's Tennessee River as the Mississippi. While it does not show the location of Fort Loudon or other British outposts, it does show the location of a set of waterfalls on today's Hiwassee River in eastern Tennessee. British colonial officials believed that these falls represented the closest point to the Carolina colonies that French traders and soldiers coming from the Ohio River might reach by boat. The British feared that French incursions could win the Cherokee away from their existing alliance with the British. Our copy of this map bears the pencilled notes "1760" and "$5.00," indicating that this copy had been offered for sale on the antiquarian market."

In the years after the Civil War, Thaddeus M. Fowler was the most prolific of a small group of itinerant viewmakers who traveled the country to capture its boom towns, villages, and cities in such lithographed ""bird's eye"" prints, making a living selling these print maps to proud citizens who'd pre-ordered. Far in advance of any prospective settlement--the land would not come open by treaty for settlement until around 1820, this particular tract was on the Reelfoot River in northwest Tennessee, near what became Reelfoot Lake after the 1811-1812 New Madrid earthquakes. John Gray and Thomas Blount were two of the most prolific land speculators in early Tennessee. oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:title: Plot of rebel fortifications made 1861 at Mill Springs Ky. encamped by Felix K. Zollicoffer Brig. Gen. Comdg. C.S. Vol.
oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:description: Hand-drawn map of Mill Springs, Kentucky made during the Civil War and showing the disposition of Confederate units. The map shows the Cumberland River, Monticello Road, S[o]merset Road, and Confederate fortifications. The town of Mill Springs and Robertsport are stylized and details of Robertsport include the grocery and a clothing store. The title ""Plat of Rebel Fortifications"" suggests the map was drawn by a Union witness.

The Battle of Mill Springs (or Fishing Creek, as it was sometimes known) took place on January 19, 1862 and was a complete Union victory. Brigadier General Felix K. Zollicoffer led Major General Crittendon's first brigade to fortify the Cumberland Gap in September 1861. By November, Zollicoffer had moved his troops into Kentucky and established a fortified position on the Cumberland River. On the morning of January 19, Zollicoffer and his men--many of whom were armed with old flintlock muskets, which would not fire in the rain--launched an attack on the Union troops, commanded by Brigadier General George H. Thomas. With poor visibility due to darkness, smoke, and his own myopia, Zollicoffer, in his white raincoat, led the vanguard and mistakenly approached enemy troops. He was mortally wounded, becoming the first Confederate general to die in the West. After his death, his soldiers panicked and fled the battle.

These include Tuscumbia, York, Florence, Bainbridge, Courtland, and Marathon. oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:title: Map of Pennsylvania (1826)
oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:description: This spectacular map of Pennsylvania is one of the crowning achievements of early American cartography. It is hand colored along county and state borders, showing the counties of Pennsylvania and the surrounding states including, New Jersey, and parts of Delaware, Maryland, Virginia, Ohio, New York, and the District of Columbia. Geographic features such as rivers, creeks, lakes, bays, mountains, and the Atlantic Ocean are denoted. The legend indicates county lines, township lines, common roads, turnpike roads, sinking springs, heads of canoe navigation, heads of boat navigation, manufactories, mills, furnaces and forges, minerals, churches, post offices, and cities. A statistical table detailing each county's' population, land area, number of towns and post offices is at the bottom center of the map. Information regarding the creator of each county map used to make the larger map is a the bottom left. The cartouche at the top right depicts the state seal of Pennsylvania.

John Melish, a Scottish cartographer, moved to the United States in 1811. Shortly thereafter he began a cartography business and published his first map, along with Henry Tanner, in 1813, depicting the War of 1812. After the war, he began work on a comprehensive map of the United States and, with consultation from Thomas Jefferson, produced the first American-made map showing America from coast to coast. In the late 1810s and early 1820s he produced many state maps simultaneously with his nation-wide ones. He is considered to be one of, if not the most important of the early mapmakers in America. His map of the United States, first published in 1816, visualized the continentalist belief held by many Americans during this era. The map was used as a propaganda piece in the "manifest destiny" era of the 1840s. He was appointed by Pennsylvania in 1816 to create a detailed state map. With the help of many deputy surveyors, it took Melish eight years and cost the state over $30,000 to produce this map, often considered his best work.
oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:creator: Melish, John, 1771-1822

Martin Armstrong, one of the surveyors on this entry, was notable for his involvement in land speculation and devising the plan for Clarksville, Tennessee in 1784. oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:title: Battle of Brandywine in which the rebels were defeated, September the 11th. 1777, by the army under the command of General Sr. Willm. Howe
oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:description: A 1778 London-published map showing the Revolutionary War Battle of Brandywine, a debacle for Gen. Washington and the American cause which led directly to the loss of Philadelphia and the hard winter quarters at Valley Forge. Indicates troop postion and movement throughout the day-long battle. Hand-colored troop designations are as follows: Americans (Rebels) in gold, British in red, and Hessians and Anspachers in blue. Roads, rivers, headquarters,the Birmingham Meeting house, and the town of Dilworth are all denoted. Relief shown by hachures. Ferguson's riflemen are specifically designated.

The Battle of Brandywine took place on September 11, 1777, and was the largest battle of the Revolutionary War. General George Washington and approximately 14,600 troops stood in the way of General William Howe and Philadelphia. Under cover of fog, Lieut. Gen. Knyphausen led a feinting maneuver at Chadds Ford while the bulk of Howe's forces, led by Gen. Cornwallis, attacked Washington's right flank. Washington was severely outmaneuvered by this advance on his right as most of his troops were defending the ford. Maj. Gen. John Sullivan was sent to meet Cornwallis, while Brig. Gen Anthony Wayne covered Knyphausen's advance. Washington and Nathanael Greene arrived later in the day to reinforce Sullivan but the damage was done. The Americans suffered 1300 casualties, while the British sustained just under 600. Washington retreated to Philadelphia and the Continental Congress was forced to flee the city. This battle put Washington under severe scrutiny for his failures, and shortly after the fall of Philadelphia on September 26, 1777, the Conway Cabal attempted to relieve him of command. The Continental Army spent the winter of 1777-1778 at Valley Forge.

Chattanooga, which comes from Cherokee describing a creek in the area, is Hamilton County's seat of government and largest city. John Ross, a half-Cherokee, half-white man set up a ferry on the Tennessee River called Ross's Landing or Ross's Ferry in 1816, and the city grew around it, changing its name to Chattanooga in 1839. Griffith Morgan Hopkins was born around 1836, however the exact date is unknown. He first began printing maps in 1857 and continued until his retirement in 1900. He founded G. M. Hopkins & Co. with his brother Henry W. Hopkins, and together they produced many city and county atlases, primarily of the northeast, from their shop in Philadelphia. G. M. Hopkins & Co. continued on after the founders' retirements until the Great Depression ended the demand for their atlases. The company was sold to the Franklin Survey Company in 1943, with the name intact, due to its association with quality.

oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:title: State of Tennessee coal fields and producing districts (1919)
oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:description: This U.S. Geological Survey map of Tennessee illustrates the coal fields of the Cumberland Plateau in the early 1900s. Areas underlain by coal bearing rocks are shown in tan and principal coal producing districts are shown in red, with the names of large coal fields indicated by name. The map shows the states' counties, including cities, towns, railroads, rivers, and creeks.

Coal mining in Tennessee first began in the 1840s. However, it did not become an important industry until after the Civil War, when railroad construction made it easier for miners to reach deposits and for coal to reach cities. In the 1870s, Tennessee was tenth in bituminous, or soft, coal production, with output primarily in plateau counties. Around this time, investors purchased huge tracts of land and controlled the most fruitful mines. From 1909 to 1939, coal was the most valuable mineral resource in Tennessee. Production burgeoned during World War II and again in the 1970s, topping out at 11.2 million tons in 1972. During this time, Tennessee ranked eleventh nationally in production, but by the 1990s the value of coal production had fallen by approximately 66%.

oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:title: The Watauga[h] land purchases
oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:description: Printed map showing the Watauga land purchases in Sullivan and Washington counties that accompanies a book by the same name. These were the earliest conveyances--March, 1775--from Native Americans, in this case Cherokee headmen including Oconostota and Attakullakulla, to white settlers in what is now Tennessee. Grantees included such prominent settlers as William Bean, John Carter, James and Charles Robertson, and John and Valentine Sevier. Their plats are overlaid on a current map of the area centered on Johnson City and Elizabethton, TN. The plats are numbered and an accompanying table details the owners of said plats. The legend denotes streams, lakes, rivers, county boundaries, state boundaries, plats, and cities.

The earliest white European settlers in Tennessee came to the northeast region of the state, the most easily accessible by river routes from Virginia and North Carolina. They generally resided near a water source so the Holston, Nolichucky, and Watauga rivers and their tributaries became their homesteads. The Watuaga River was centrally located among the three and thus lent its name to these settlements. These settlers emigrated to the area in violation of the Proclamation of 1763 and had to lease their land from the Cherokee. They eventually formed their own government, the Watauga Association, and petitioned the state of North Carolina for protection and the benefits of government.

oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:title: Carte de Kentucke, d'après les Observations actuelles Dédiée a L'Honorable Congrès des Etats Unis de l'Amérique et à Son Excellence George Washington, Commandant en chef de les Armées (1785)
oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:description: John Filson's French language map of the central "bluegrass" part of Kentucky Territory published in his Histoire de Kentucke, 1785. Bounded by the Ohio, Cumberland and Green (Riviere Verte) Rivers, it shows cities and towns, Native American villages, rivers, creeks, mountains, counties, and includes commentary on certain features. Centered on the early settled area around Lexington, Harrods Town, and Boonsborough, this map names forts, salt works and springs, towns, dwellings and mills (moulins), and "cabones des sauvages," or cabins of the savages, referring to Native Americans. Early migration routes are noted, such as the roads (chemins) leading to the Cumberland settlements around Nashville and the long-established one between Virginia and Kentucky. Particular attention is given to the quality of the land as indicated by prairie or the presence of cane and the location of workable salt deposits. The mill of Col. [Daniel] Boon[e] and the fort of Col. [Isaac] Shelby, among many other named establishments, are shown.

Filson's original map (and book) was published in English the year prior to this French translation, and eventually into German. This work, like many early maps and guidebooks from the American frontier, highlighted the advantages of moving to the new territory of Kentucky, specifically the mineral resources, farmland, and modes of transportation. Filson, as a close friend of Daniel Boone, added an appendix which publicized Boone's accomplishments.

oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:title: A map of Indian boundary lines and the southern boundary of the state of Tennessee (1807)
oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:description: Hand-drawn map showing the boundary line of the Chickasaw Treaty of 1806, drawn by the surveyor of said treaty, Thomas Freeman. In addition to the Chickasaw boundary line, the map also indicates the Tennessee Congressional line, the Cherokee boundary line, the new southern boundary line of Tennessee, and the Huntsville meridian (the line from which all township and range lines are drawn in the state of Alabama). The Tennessee River, Elk River, Duck River, Flint River, Richland Creek, and Muscle Shoals are included. Cherokee Mountains, and the dividing ridge between the waters of Buffalo and Duck rivers are artistically shown. The "Barrens" of lower middle Tennessee are indicated as are a large swamp near present-day Huntsville, and "Doublehead's Place." This map may contain the earliest representation of the Huntsville meridian and Madison County, Alabama [Mississippi Territory] "Run & marked, Sept. 1807."

Thomas Freeman was born in Ireland and moved to the United States in 1784. He served as land agent to George Washington in the 1790s, surveying his land and collecting rents. After Pierre L'Enfant and Andrew Ellicott resigned from laying out Washington D. C. Freeman completed the necessary surveying. In 1795 he was appointed by George Washington to survey the 31st parallel, to serve as the boundary between American and Spanish possessions following the Pinckney Treaty. Freeman was appointed to lead the Red River Expedition, also known as the Freeman-Custis Expedition, in 1806, to explore the lower Louisiana Territory. After completion of the failed mission, Freeman was appointed to survey the recently negotiated Chickasaw Treaty of 1806 in lower Tennessee and northern Alabama (known as Mississippi Territory). This map appears to be a relic of this undertaking. In 1810, Freeman was appointed Surveyor-General of the Mississippi Territory and remained in Alabama until his death in 1821. He is buried at Maple Hill Cemetery in Huntsville, Alabama.

oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:title: Siege of Vera Cruz by the U. S. troops under Major General Scott, in March 1847
oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:description: Map of the siege of Vera Cruz during the Mexican-American War. Vera Cruz, and its surrounding forts, is shown with roads leading to and from the town. The amphibious landing location is noted, as is the troop positions of the various divisions led by Worth, Twigg, and Patterson. The headquarters of each general are noted as are the depots, batteries, and entrenchments. Naval guns were taken off the American ships and used to reduce Mexican positions. The 1st and 2nd regiments of Tennessee Volunteers were engaged on the center-right of the American's ""line of investment."" A small table containing casualty numbers is located in the bottom right. Presented by Major Adolphus Heiman [presumably to the Tennessee Historical Society], May 4, 1858.

On March 9, 1847, American troops performed their first major amphibious operation, landing 12,000 men, supplies, weapons, and horses at Vera Cruz, Mexico. After the 12-day siege of the city, the Mexicans surrendered. Scott's troops continued their campaign toward Mexico City and met Mexican troops under General Santa Anna entrenched near Cerro Gordo. After a decisive victory, the Americans marched on to Puebla, who surrendered without resistance. After the Battles of Contreras, Churubusco, Molino del Rey, and Chapultepec, Santa Anna withdrew to Guadalupe Hidalgo. After a 5 month guerilla campaign, the war ended there with the signing of the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo on February 2, 1848. The treaty ceded California, Nevada, Utah, and parts of New Mexico, Arizona, Texas, Oklahoma, Kansas, Wyoming, and Colorado to the United States for $15 million. Many generals in the Civil War participated in the Mexican War, specifically the Mexico City campaign including: Robert E. Lee, George Meade, Ulysses S. Grant, James Longstreet, Thomas ""Stonewall"" Jackson, Gideon J. Pillow, Joseph E. Johnston, Sterling Price, George B. McClellan, Daniel H. Hill, and George Pickett. Future Tennessee governor William Trousdale served as a Colonel in this campaign.

oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:title: Verdun (1911)
oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:description: Extremely detailed French topographic map showing a portion of the Meuse department to the west and north of the town of Verdun. Based on an 1835 War Department map and revised in 1911, it names every wood (""bois"") and enclosed field (""ferme"") and a great many place-names; such maps were used for military operations. Farmland, forest, rivers, and hills make up the landscape. Roads, railroads, dwellings, and forts are indicated. Scale 1:80,000. Plate 35. Little of the battlefield for the catastrophic 1916 Battle of Verdun is shown, since most of it lay off-map to the east of the town and Meuse River. However, this map does show a small portion of the road to the southwest that would become the famous Voie Sacree, the re-supply route that saved the French stand at Verdun.

Fought from February 21 to December 16, 1916, Verdun was one of the largest and bloodiest battles of World War I. Over 2 million French and German troops engaged one another for 10 months, fired over 10 million shells, and suffered almost a million casualties. This map was produced earlier than World War I (rev. 1911) but is included in a scrapbook of World War I materials belonging to Jacob McGavock Dickinson Jr. presumably while in military service in France.

oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:title: Sanborn Fire Insurance Map of Nashville, Tenn. (1914, rev. 1931)
oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:description: This is a Sanborn fire insurance map showing the the areas bound by 17th Avenue, 14th Avenue, Church St., and Cedar (Charlotte Ave.) in Nashville, Tenn. [Vol. 1 Page 19 and 20 of 1914 series, rev. 1931] It includes churches, apartments and businesses. Filling and service stations, negro tenements, a playground, a drug store, the Bethlehem Center Training School and gymnasium, the Capers Memorial Church, and the Biggins Commercial College are all denoted. Much of the area on Plate 19 shows the contemporary area of the location of the old state prison, remnants include prison alley. Details include outlines of each building, the location of windows and doors, property boundaries, firewalls, types of building materials used, heat sources, light sources and electric, locations of fire hydrants, location of water and gas mains, etc.

Daniel Alfred Sanborn, a civil engineer and surveyor, began working on fire insurance maps in the 1860s and his company soon became one of the largest and most successful American map companies. Sanborn's first work mapping cities for insurance purposes began in Tennessee when Aetna Insurance hired him to survey a few towns across the state, however none of these earliest examples are known to exist today (Ristow, Walter W. "United States Fire Insurance and Underwriters Maps· 1852—1968." The Quarterly Journal of the Library of Congress 25, no. 3 (1968): 194-218." Sanborn maps were originally created to estimate fire insurance risks. Insurance companies would decide how much insurance, if any, was to be offered to a customer solely through the use of a Sanborn map. Today, the maps are frequently used for historical research and for preservation and restoration purposes.

oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:title: Nouveau plan de Paris fortifié (1855)
oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:description: Detailed map in French depicting the old city of Paris in 1855--essentially still a medieval city on the brink of Baron Haussmann's wholesale renovation. It shows streets, buildings, railroads, landmarks, neighborhoods, the Seine River, arrondissements, and the fortifications--star forts and walls--that still surrounded the city but were shortly to disappear. A street index is located to the left of the map with a "table of names omitted in the nomenclature." To the right is a building index including governmental departments, libraries, theaters, and passages.

Haussmann's 1853-1870 renovation of Paris was a vast public works program commissioned by Emperor Napoléon III and directed by his prefect of the Seine, Georges-Eugène Haussmann. It included the demolition of crowded mazes of medieval neighborhoods, the building of wide avenues ("boulevards") as spokes with parks and squares at their hubs, the annexation of the suburbs surrounding Paris, and the construction of new sewers, fountains and aqueducts. The modern street plan and distinctive appearance of the center of Paris today is largely the result of Haussmann's renovation.

oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:description: Hand-drawn map by Confederate cavalryman John Johnston detailing Confederate movements during and after the Battle of Nashville on December 16 and 17, 1864, between Hillsboro Pike and Franklin Pike, just north of the Little Harpeth River. The Federal cavalry line is indicated, as is the 14th regiment, the field of Johnston's "last stand" on December 16th, and the scene of Ben Rucker's capture. The rallying place of Gen. John Johnston was born in 1842 and joined the Confederate army in April 1861. He served in Nathan Bedford Forrest's cavalry during the war. Following the war he became a lawyer in Memphis and wrote a memoir of his experiences during the Civil War. He died in 1928.

oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:title: S. W. Territory (1795)
oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:description: Philadelphia-published map of territorial Tennessee or the Southwest Territory, formerly known as the Territory of the United States South of the River Ohio, from 1795. Knoxville, Nashville, and Clarksville are the only three white settlements shown. A number of Native American villages are indicated including Coyeta, Chota, Talasse, Cholhowee, Crow Town, Nickajack Town, Cherokee Town, and Estenauhly. The rivers are mapped in detail. Other important features shown in this map are Fort Massac, Ross's Iron Works, the boundaries of the Military Reservation (for North Carolina Revolutionary War land grants) in Middle Tennessee, as well as the three counties that make up the Mero District -- Tennessee, Davidson, and Sumner. The "Creeks crossing place" seems to be a reference to a ford near the Chickasaw Old Fields. A notation from East Tennessee southward reads "To Pensacola the way nearly level."

The area the makes up the present-day Tennessee was originally part of the colony of North Carolina, who ceded the land to the United States government to repay their Revolutionary War debts on December 22, 1789. Congress officially accepted this cession on April 2, 1790, and formally organized the Territory of the United States South of the River Ohio, or Southwest Territory, on May 26, 1790. After a statewide referendum in 1795, Tennessee voted to join the Union and was admitted on June 1, 1796. This map appears to have been the model from which Daniel Smith produced his map of the "Tennessee Government" that same year.

oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:title: A general map of the new settlement of Transilvania, November 1776 (1930 drawing)
oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:description: A map of North Carolina, Virginia, Kentucky, and Tennessee showing the area of Kentucky known as Transylvania. The map has a detailed view of rivers, towns, Cherokee, Creek, and Chickasaw villages, and forts. It specifically indicates salt and coal deposits, elephant bones, roads, the Watauga Settlements [Wotauga], Ft. Loudon, and the separate Overhill, Middle, and Lower Cherokee towns.

The Transylvania Purchase was a private venture by Richard Henderson and the Transylvania Company to obtain 20 million acres of land in present-day Kentucky and Tennessee in order to establish a 14th colony. Henderson negotiated this agreement with the Cherokee on March 14, 1775, and he, along with other settlers, drew up the Transylvania Compact, framing the fledgling government. However, his plan was thwarted when Virginia annexed the land and voided the agreement. Henderson was allowed to retain rights to 12 square miles (about 7700 acres), and thereafter attempted to settle the Tennessee portion at Nashborough.

oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:title: Map of the explored parts of the Mammoth Cave of KY. (1845)
oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:description: Map of Mammoth Cave drawn from memory by an early African American guide, Stephen Bishop. It shows the labyrinth of passages that made up the Mammoth Cave system, now considered the world's longest, as it was known in the early 19th century. It assigns colorful names to various passages, chambers and famous spots along the route. The "Rotundo" is shown, where saltpeter from the cave was processed by enslaved individuals into gunpowder for use by American troops during the War of 1812. Underground rivers are shaded and named.

Stephen Bishop was born enslaved around 1821. His owner, Franklin Gorin, purchased Mammoth Cave in 1838 and used Bishop as a guide in order to monetize his purchase. In 1839, Gorin sold the estate, Bishop included, to Dr. John Croghan. Bishop was the first known person to cross the "Bottomless Pit" and thus explore the cave beyond that point. In 1842, Croghan had Bishop draw a map of Mammoth Cave, which was eventually published in 1844. Bishop was freed in 1856, one year before his death from tuberculosis.

oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:title: A plan of that part of Whites Creek turnpike road extending from its beginning on the Gallatin Turnpike through the Lands of Shelby Washington Weakley and others (1845)
oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:description: Hand-drawn map showing the reroute of White's Creek Turnpike across the Cumberland River from Nashville in 1845. Various pond and drainage features are shown in what would later become Edgefield. The corporation limits of the City of Nashville are shown along with the Lick Branch that flowed through the old French Lick. The old White's Creek road ran along the river in what this map refers to as the river bottom. The turnpike was built upon high ground as shown on this map. The Cumberland River, Lick Branch, the Gallatin Turnpike, Dickinson meeting house road, and Nashville Bridge are depicted, as are a cabin, icehouse and well on a tract labeled Washington's Lands. The new turnpike separates the lands of James McGavock, Col. Robert Weakley, and James Crutcher. It runs through John Shelby and Thomas Washington's lands, which are shown in great detail including his cabin, well, and ice house. The proposed turnpike is located near present-day Dickerson Pike and Trinity Road. The map was drawn by White's Creek Turnpike Superintendent and later owner, C. W. Nance.
White's Creek Turnpike was given a charter of incorporation in 1830, and C. W. Nance was appointed to superintend the construction, totaling $31,000. The turnpike was finished in 1844.

oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:title: John Filson's map of Kentucke (1929 reproduction of 1785 original)
oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:description: John Filson's map of the central "bluegrass" part of Kentucky Territory published in his History of Kentucke, 1785. Bounded by the Ohio, Cumberland and Green Rivers, it shows cities and towns, Native American villages, rivers, creeks, mountains, counties, and includes commentary on certain features. Centered on the early settled area around Lexington, Harrods Town, and Boonsborough, this map names forts, salt works and springs, towns, dwellings and mills, and wigwams. Early migration routes are noted, such as the roads leading to the Cumberland settlements around Nashville and the long-established one between Virginia and Kentucky. Particular attention is given to the quality of the land as indicated by prairie or the presence of cane and the location of workable salt deposits. The mill of Col. [Daniel] Boon[e] and the fort of Col. [Isaac] Shelby, among many other named establishments, are shown. This particular copy is a reproduction of the first Philadelphia 1784 map of Kentucky by John Filson, issued to accompany "Filson's Kentucke" by Willard Rouse Jillison in 1929.

Filson's original map (and book) was published in 1794, and was later translated into French and German. This work, like many early maps and guidebooks from the American frontier, highlighted the advantages of moving to the new territory of Kentucky, specifically the mineral resources, farmland, and modes of transportation. Filson, as a close friend of Daniel Boone, added an appendix which publicized Boone's accomplishments. See Paris-published French version from 1785 http://teva.contentdm.oclc.org/cdm/singleitem/collection/p15138coll23/id/9052/rec/1

The Cumberland River flows through the middle of the map. On the east side of the river are 640 acre tracts belonging to Thomas Shaw, David McGavock, and David Ewing as well as features such as Pond Creek, Fountain Blue, Sinkhole Spring, and Pleasant Mount. oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:title: Plan of Nashville, 1805
oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:description: Hand-drawn plat map of Nashville dated 1805. This important early map shows the property owners for most of the lots in the city that were laid out by Thomas Molloy 21 years prior. The Cumberland River is positioned at the bottom of the map, with a street labeled Nashville Bridge(" and the Public Square nearby. Some recognizable lot owners include Hardy Murfree, James Robertson, John Boyd, Martin Armstrong, Elijah Robertson, William Blount, John Rice, William Crutcher, Aubrey Crutcher, John Cockrill, Andrew Ewing, Russell Gower, James Thompson, Bennett Searcy, Boyd McNairy, John Overton, James Shaw, Thomas Deaderick, and Timothy Demonbreun, among others. The original street names and grid are shown. A a seemingly anachronistic note about a bridge is handwritten across the Cumberland River.

Robert Searcy was an early Nashville attorney. He served as treasurer for the Mero District from 1797 to 1803, was appointed justice of the peace for Davidson County in 1799, served as alderman of Nashville from 1806 to 1809, served as trustee of Davidson Academy, and clerk of federal district court in Nashville. He and his brother, William owned a mercantile business in Nashville from 1802 until 1806. Searcy freed the enslaved Robert Renfro[e], in 1801, who went on to become an important free black entrepreneur in Nashville.

oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:title: Old Stone Fort near Manchester, Tennessee
oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:description: 19th century published map of the area near the so-called Old Stone Fort, a major Woodland prehistoric site near Manchester, Tennessee. Despite the name, reflecting early confusion among antiquarians about the origin and character of these native earthen works, Old Stone Fort at the fork of the Duck and the Little Duck Rivers was not a fortification. It was likely a ceremonial or gathering spot for southeastern native Americans some 1500-2000 years BP, as well as an historic mill site during the 1800s. Old Stone Fort is drawn on 40 acres within "walls" with an associated "ancient canal," "ancient stone dam," and "ancient mound." Nearby waterfalls, mill dams, and caves are denoted. The McMinnville [and Manchester] Railroad is shown as is the McMinnville Road, the Murfreesboro Road, Woodbury Road, and Mill Road. The town of Manchester is drawn along with the town spring and railroad depot.

The map's author, Alexander Kocsis, was a Hungarian immigrant and one of the first to argue that Old Stone Fort was a native American creation and that it had ceremonial rather than military significance. The site contains a Middle Woodland period earthen enclosure in Coffee County, Tennessee. Originally thought to have been constructed by the Spanish under de Soto, radiocarbon dating showed that it was built closer to 2,000 years ago.

Shows the Sandy [Big Sandy River]and Tennessee River and denotes the location of Paris. Map and field call description of civil district boundaries.

These 1836 county maps showing the new civil districts, required by the recent state constitution (written in 1834 and ratified the following year), which mandated such civil divisions for taxation and election purposes, were done for many counties. Henry County was established in 1821 from lands purchased from the Chickasaw in 1818, known as the Jackson Purchase or Chickasaw Purchase. It is named for patriot, author, and orator Patrick Henry. its county seat and largest city is Paris, named for the French capital supposedly to honor the Marquis de Lafayette.

oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:description: World War II newsmap showing various global combat theatres or fronts, including the coastal geography of the D-Day invasion of Normandy on June 6, 1944. The two smaller flanking maps depict the Schoutten Islands north of Dutch New Guinea, and the Italian front, specifically troop movements near Rome. Updates from the various fronts accompany the map. An infantry-boosting US Army promotional poster on verso.

TSLA holds a large collection of these WWII ""newsmaps"" detailing for the American public the weekly events of US military efforts in Europe and the Pacific theaters. The Bureau of Public Relations was established in the Office of the Secretary of War in February 1941.The Bureau served as the central War Department agency to determine policies and procedures for disseminating military information to the public. After August 1942, it was also responsible for the public relations activities of the Army Air Forces, the Army Service Forces and the Army Ground Forces. During the war, the Bureau produced these weekly newsmaps for War Department distribution.
