oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:title: School atlas to Cummings' Ancient and modern geography
oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:description: An 1820s school atlas, signed and presumably owned by Samuel Donelson of Nashville (Tenn." The first page shows a map of the world with national boundaries hand colored, with the United States stretching only as far west as the Mississippi River and not including Spanish Florida. The second page depicts North America and includes Native American tribes, states, cities, forts, rivers, and lakes. The third shows only the United States with hand colored state borders. Towns, rivers, mountains, and forts are drawn. The fourth depicts South America and includes provincial borders, towns, rivers, and missions. The fifth shows Europe with national borders hand colored, cities, towns, rivers, and mountains. The sixth is a more detailed look at the United Kingdom, once again featuring cities, towns, rivers, and lakes. The seventh and final is of Asia with hand colored national borders and depicting towns, cities, rivers, mountains, and islands. Handwriting can be seen on verso of most maps. The map of Africa is missing.

Bettie Mizell was born in Nashville, Tennessee in 1862. In 1882, she married William Alexander Donelson, son of diplomat and vice presidential nominee Andrew Jackson Donelson. William was murdered on July 21, 1900, by William Giles Baker after a long standing dispute. Bettie was one of the primary founders of the Ladies Hermitage Association, participated in the women's suffrage movement, and helped develop the plan for the Woman�s Department of the Tennessee Centennial. After her husband's death, Bettie served as Chairman of Davidson County Woman�s Christian Temperance Union and Chairman of the General Arrangements Committee when the national convention met in Nashville in 1907. She served as president of the Andrew Jackson Society in the 1920s and 30s and was a delegate to the World Conference of Women in Washington, D. C. in 1923. She died in 1939.

oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:title: Virginia, Marylandia et Carolina in America septentrionali Britannorum (approximately 1759)
oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:description: Early German map of colonial America on excellent hand-made paper that shows among other things the early settlements of tidewater Virginia, the Chesapeake and the Carolinas. It includes many major geographical errors: the northern coastline is skewed, Lake Erie is shown too far south and massively oversized, Florida stretches from the south all the way to Lake Erie. The Apalache Lake, a common early feature referencing a native Floridian tribe, is located in North Carolina's interior. Meister Krug's plantation and Germantown Teutsche Statt appear as possible destinations for potential German immigrants. Also covers New Jersey, Southern Pennsylvania, and New York City region. Includes illustrations. Relief shown pictorially. Depths shown by soundings. The elaborate cartouche depicts trade with the natives, colorful depictions of natives, fish, sea monsters, a shipping warehouse (filled with tobacco or hams), and a seal with the phrase ""honi soit qui mal y pense,"" meaning ""May he be shamed who thinks badly of it,"" which also appears on John Smith's 1612 map of Virginia. In Homann's Atlas Geographicvs Maior, produced from 1714-1759.

This map was drawn by Johann Baptist Homann to attract German immigrants to America. Virginia Colony governor, Alexander Spotswood, wanted to attract immigrants to settle the frontier, so he built Fort Christiana [Christ Anna fort] in 1714 as a buffer from and teaching facility for the American Indians.

oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:title: A Map of the Southern Section of the United States including The Floridas and Bahama Islands Showing the Seat of War in that Department (1813)
oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:description: John Melish's map of the southern theater of the War of 1812. State and national borders are denoted and hand-colored. Highly detailed view of the rivers, roads, and forts throughout the Southeast, including a detailed rendering of the Natchez Trace with mileage markers. Towns, settlements, and Native American villages are shown, as are tribal lands. Important sites of the Creek War in the Mississippi Territory, such as Ft. Strother, Ft. Deposit, McGil[le]vray Town and McIntoshville, are shown. Annotations such as "Pike's exploring party stop[p]ed here" and "The alligators go no further north" are found in the Louisiana and Missouri territories. Indian boundary lines are visible in Illinois and Indiana territories.

John Melish, a Scottish cartographer, moved to the United States in 1811. Shortly thereafter he began a cartography business and published his first map, along with Henry Tanner, in 1813, depicting the War of 1812. After the war, he began work on a comprehensive map of the United States and, with consultation from Thomas Jefferson, produced the first American-made map showing America from coast to coast. In the late 1810s and early 1820s he produced many state maps simultaneously with his nation-wide ones. He is considered to be one of, if not the most important of the early mapmakers in America. His map of the United States, first published in 1816, visualized the continentalist belief held by many Americans during this era. The map was used as a propaganda piece in the "manifest destiny" era of the 1840s.

oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:title: Survey of the Cumberland River from the Falls to Nashville, Sheets I-V (1834)
oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:description: Detailed survey of the Cumberland River from the Falls near Barbourville, Kentucky to the Great South Fork [Big South Fork] drawn by civil engineers as an aid in identifying and clearing the river of shallow obstructions for steamboats. Shallows and shoals are specifically denoted and their depths measured and set aside as charts above the map. Coal mines, bituminous and limestone strata, and river landings are indicated. Arrows denoting the flow of the river are included. This map is a more detailed subset of the larger Cumberland River survey at http://teva.contentdm.oclc.org/cdm/singleitem/collection/p15138coll23/id/18/rec/2

Such river survey maps were produced in the 19th century by engineers attached to War Department as precursors to the modern activities of the US Army Corps of Engineers. Their concern was with the constitutional requirement for the Federal government to facilitate navigation and commerce on navigable rivers by dredging and clearing obstructions to--at this time--steamboat traffic.

John Rice was granted 5,000 acres along the Mississippi River on the Fourth Chickasaw Bluff in 1789 by the state of North Carolina. John Overton purchased it from Rice's brother Elisha Rice in 1794 for £1,000. Overton sold half of the tract to Andrew Jackson, who sold a portion of his claim to James Winchester for $5,000. The land along the river was set aside as public land to lay out the city of Memphis.

oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:title: Kentucky and Tennessee (1855)
oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:description: Map of Kentucky and Tennessee with hand colored counties. Cities, towns, rivers, and railroads are all denoted. Colton's distinctive border design is visible around the map. Township and range grids are evident where applicable. Both this and the 1854 version are identical and depict the state of Tennessee prior to 1854, before the re-creation of Putnam County.

J. H. Colton was born in England in 1800 and immigrated to New York City in the 1830s. His first foray into mapmaking involved purchasing the rights to other's work rather than creating his own. By the 1840s Colton was producing his own, and by 1860 his General Atlas was ubiquitous. His two sons G.W. and C.B. following in his footsteps and joined the family business. In 1857 they were commissioned to create an atlas of Bolivia, but upon completion, they refused payment. He was eventually able to recoup payment after a prolonged legal battle, but this setback coupled with the Panic of 1857, forced him to have to go into business and sell his plates to Alvin Jewett Johnson and Ross C. Browning, who became direct competitors. J. H Colton retired from cartography in 1865 and died in 1893.

oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:description: This map, showing the alignment of Allied and German forces on July 23, 1918, was found at the Alvin C. York site and may have belonged to York. It depicts the entire Argonne Forest sector over which the American 82nd Div., including York's Co. G, 328th Inf. Regt., attacked German positions in late 1918. The map shows Hill 223 north of Chatel-Chehery where, on Oct. 8, York and a detachment took out a nest of enemy machine guns and captured 132 German soldiers, for which he received the Medal of Honor.

The Meuse-Argonne Offensive, also known as the Battle of the Argonne Forest, was a part of the final Allied offensive of World War I that stretched along the entire Western Front. It was fought from September 26, 1918, until the Armistice on November 11.

oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:title: Plat of John Rice tract (approximately 1824)
oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:description: Plat showing the division of the 5,000 acre John Rice tract on the Fourth Chickasaw Bluff that would later be the site of Memphis, Tennessee. This division was between the three men credited with being the founders of Memphis--John Overton, Andrew Jackson, and James Winchester. John Rice, a land speculator, had bought the warrant for this North Carolina grant from Secretary of State John Armstrong's office in the 1780s when this land was Indian territory. Rice was murdered by the Cherokee warrior Doublehead in 1792, long before this part of West Tennessee was opened for settlement by Jackson's treaty with the Chickasaw in 1818.

John Rice was granted 5,000 acres along the Mississippi River on the Fourth Chickasaw Bluff in 1789 by the state of North Carolina. John Overton purchased it from Rice's brother Elisha Rice in 1794 for £1,000. Overton sold half of the tract to Andrew Jackson, who sold a portion of his claim to James Winchester for $5,000. The land along the river was set aside as public land to lay out the city of Memphis.

oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:title: Tennessee
oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:description: Color map of Tennessee from showing towns, roads, different-colored counties, streams and railroads. Still shows range-and-section grid patterns from land grant system in West Tennessee and old Hiawassee and Ocoee Districts. Includes portions of adjacent states. Shows railroads completed, railroads proposed, and wagon roads.

J. H. Colton was born in England in 1800 and immigrated to New York City in the 1830s. His first foray into mapmaking involved purchasing the rights to other's work rather than creating his own. By the 1840s Colton was producing his own, and by 1860 his General Atlas was ubiquitous. His two sons G.W. and C.B. following in his footsteps and joined the family business. In 1857 they were commissioned to create an atlas of Bolivia, but upon completion, they refused payment. He was eventually able to recoup payment after a prolonged legal battle, but this setback coupled with the Panic of 1857, forced him to have to go into business and sell his plates to Alvin Jewett Johnson and Ross C. Browning, who became direct competitors. J. H Colton retired from cartography in 1865 and died in 1893.

oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:description: Andrew Jackson's handwritten, official report of the Battle of Horseshoe Bend to Governor Willie Blount. Gen. Jackson goes into considerable detail about his approach to the Red Stick Creek's fortified bend of the Tallapoosa River, which "barbarians have never rendered...more secure by art." Jackson specifically commends the conduct of his Cherokee allies, "headed by their gallant Chieftain Col. Richard Brown." A hand-drawn map depicting the battle prefaces the written report, in which Jackson gives a blow-by-blow account of the battle and its aftermath. Horseshoe Bend was a decisive victory for Jackson's Tennesseans--the "slaughter" he says, "was suspended only by the darkness of night"--and Creek military power was broken.

Ramsey and various early Claiborne County, Tenn. deeds. Used to accompany Ramsey's description of the Transylvania Purchase in these river valleys. Also includes the Claiborne County deed text. Located in a box on top of map cases with oversized maps.

The Transylvania Purchase was a private venture by Richard Henderson and the Transylvania Company to obtain 20 million acres of land in present-day Kentucky and Tennessee in order to establish a 14th colony. Henderson negotiated this agreement with the Cherokee on March 14, 1775, and he, along with other settlers, drew up the Transylvania Compact, framing the fledgling government. However, his plan was thwarted when Virginia annexed the land and voided the agreement. Henderson was allowed to retain rights to 12 square miles (about 7700 acres), and thereafter attempted to settle the Tennessee portion at Nashborough.

Hugh Lawson White Hill was born in Warren County on March 1, 1810. He graduated from Cumberland College and went on to serve in the Tennessee General Assembly from 1837 to 1843. In 1890, E. E. Meacham acquired land that had been part of Deaderick Plantation. He built a segregated neighborhood, Orange Mound, for African American homeowners, named after the Osage Orange hedges that had lined the Deaderick Plantation. The neighborhood originally contained 982 shotgun houses. Living in Orange Mound became something of a status symbol among black Memphians because one could own rather than rent a house. The neighborhood itself fostered a strong sense of community and identity.

oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:title: Sanborn Fire Insurance Map of Nashville, Tenn. (1897, rev. 1911)
oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:description: This is a Sanborn fire insurance map showing the section between Ewing Ave and 8th Ave. in downtown Nashville, Tenn. [Vol. II Pages 131-132 of 1897 series, rev. 1911] It includes churches, houses and residences, and businesses. Notable are the Academy of the Immaculate Mother, a private Catholic school for African American children, and the Florence Crit[t]enton Mission Home for Girls.

Daniel Alfred Sanborn, a civil engineer and surveyor, began working on fire insurance maps in the 1860s and his company soon became one of the largest and most successful American map companies. Sanborn's first work mapping cities for insurance purposes began in Tennessee when Aetna Insurance hired him to survey a few towns across the state, however none of these earliest examples are known to exist today (Ristow, Walter W. "United States Fire Insurance and Underwriters Maps· 1852—1968." The Quarterly Journal of the Library of Congress 25, no. 3 (1968): 194-218." Sanborn maps were originally created to estimate fire insurance risks. Insurance companies would decide how much insurance, if any, was to be offered to a customer solely through the use of a Sanborn map. Today, the maps are frequently used for historical research and for preservation and restoration purposes.

oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:title: A map of the most inhabited part of Virginia
oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:description: This exhaustive map of the Mid-Atlantic region shows the cities, towns, roads, courthouses, mills, camps, forts, mines, and trade routes of the area. Geographic features include rivers, creeks, mountains, springs, bays, islands, swamps, and inlets. Some landowners are denoted. The map was the first to depict the parallel ranges of the Appalachian Mountains, and the headwaters of the Catawba and Yadkin rivers in North Carolina. The cartouche, often considered among the most attractive of the 18th century, depicts Virginia's tobacco trade on many levels, from enslaved labor, to drying and warehousing, to selling and shipping across the Atlantic.

The Fry-Jefferson map was a landmark in early American mapmaking. It is the most important 18th century map of the Mid-Atlantic region for its detail, depiction of the Virginia and North Carolina waterways, and delineation of the Appalachian Mountains. Joshua Fry was a surveyor and mathematics professor at William and Mary. Peter Jefferson was a surveyor and mapmaker, and the father of President Thomas Jefferson. Around 1750, George Dunk, the Earl of Halifax, and the Board of Trade requested a detailed map of the Virginia colony, so Governor Lewis Burwell commissioned Fry and Jefferson to complete the task. The Board of Trade paid the pair £150 for their work. Thomas Jefferys originally published the map in 1753 on four copper plates. This edition is from 1775 and printed in Jefferys's American Atlas on two plates. Francis Hayman and Charles Grignion engraved the cartouche. (Farrell, Cassandra Britt. Fry-Jefferson Map of Virginia. Encyclopedia Virginia."(Cumming, William P. The Southeast in Early Maps. University of North Carolina Press.)

oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:description: This massive and incredibly detailed map depicts British possessions in the New World after the French and Indian War. Geographic features include rivers, lakes, creeks, capes, inlets, islands, and mountains. Annotations describe details specifically noted in articles of the Treaty of Paris, 1763. The cartouche is one of the finest examples published in the 18th century. It depicts a pair of native people and a child, one petting a large cat. An alligator or crocodile appears to their left.

Thomas Pownall was born in 1722. He served as colonial governor of New Jersey and Massachusetts Bay, often advocating colonial positions on taxation and other controversial legislation. Pownall's American sympathies saw him voted out of office in 1774. During the Revolutionary War, Pownall worked to revise Lewis Evans map of the American colonies, resulting in this incredibly detailed masterpiece. Pownall died in 1805.

Jean Baptiste Bourguignon d'Anville was born in Paris in 1697. He published his first map at the age of fifteen, and was appointed as a geographer to the King of France by the age of twenty-two. He avoided the common practice of copying earlier maps and often performed empirical study of the land. He died in 1782.

oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:title: Nashville in 1804
oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:description: From the recollections of Mrs. Harriet Temple the daughter of Duncan Robertson. Shows Nashville in 1804 with landscape, dwellings, businesses and the Cumberland River. Eichbaum also lightly noted some present day streets as they were at the time of the creation of the map, presumably to give viewers some current reference points. Some of the referenced buildings include Talbot Tavern, Old Stone Tavern, Judge McNairy's, the former fort, Dr. Henning's house, the Court House, and various stores and guesthouses. A numbered key is located at the bottom.

William A. Eichbaum was born in Dublin, Ireland in April 1787. His father was a German immigrant, who worked in Ireland as a glass maker. William immigrated to America around 1820, after a brief journey to Peru. In 1825, he married Catharine M. Stearns, a teacher at Nashville Female Academy. Eichbaum became one of Nashville's foremost booksellers in the mod-19th century. He participated in many philanthropic and societal organizations including the Davidson County Bible Society, Horticultural Society, Nashville Historical Society, Mount Olivet Cemetery Company, and Nashville Savings Company. He died on January 1, 1873. (Letter from J. D. Eichbaum to Anson Nelson, T-100 Collection, Tennessee Historical Society) Eichbaum's sketchbook is housed at Nashville Public Library and contains another version of this map.

Griffith Morgan Hopkins was born around 1836, however the exact date is unknown. He first began printing maps in 1857 and continued until his retirement in 1900. He founded G. M. Hopkins & Co. with his brother Henry W. Hopkins, and together they produced many city and county atlases, primarily of the northeast, from their shop in Philadelphia. Their 1908 Atlas of Nashville is a fine, block-by-block depiction of the town in a period of growth to a modern urban center. G. M. Hopkins & Co. continued on after the founders' retirements until the Great Depression ended the demand for their atlases. The company was sold to the Franklin Survey Company in 1943, with the name intact, due to its association with quality.

oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:title: Map of the field of Shiloh, near Pittsburgh Landing, Tenn.
oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:description: This map includes federal troop positions for Grant's Army of the Tennessee and Buell's Army of the Ohio for the morning and evenings of April 6 and April 7. The various creeks, roads, homes, hospitals, Shiloh Church, the cotton press, Pittsburgh Landing, and the gunboats Tyler and Lexington are all included.

After successive defeats in northern Tennessee, the Confederate army regrouped in Corinth, Mississippi, under Generals Albert Sidney Johnston and P. G. T. Beauregard, as the Army of Mississippi. On April 6, 1862, it made a surprise attack on the Union’s Army of the Tennessee under the command of General Ulysses S. Grant at Pittsburg Landing, Tennessee. Later known as the Battle of Shiloh, this was deadliest battle in American history up to that date. The surprise paid off initially, as Union troops were put on the defensive. However, the arrival of Union General Don Carlos Buell proved to be the turning point as the Confederate forces were routed, amassing over ten thousand casualties.

John Rice was granted 5,000 acres along the Mississippi River on the Fourth Chickasaw Bluff in 1789 by the state of North Carolina. John Overton purchased it from Rice's brother Elisha Rice in 1794 for £1,000. Overton sold half of the tract to Andrew Jackson, who sold a portion of his claim to James Winchester for $5,000. The land along the river was set aside as public land to lay out the city of Memphis.

Daniel Alfred Sanborn, a civil engineer and surveyor, began working on fire insurance maps in the 1860s and his company soon became one of the largest and most successful American map companies. Sanborn's first work mapping cities for insurance purposes began in Tennessee when Aetna Insurance hired him to survey a few towns across the state, however none of these earliest examples are known to exist today (Ristow, Walter W. "United States Fire Insurance and Underwriters Maps· 1852—1968." The Quarterly Journal of the Library of Congress 25, no. 3 (1968): 194-218." Sanborn maps were originally created to estimate fire insurance risks. Insurance companies would decide how much insurance, if any, was to be offered to a customer solely through the use of a Sanborn map. Today, the maps are frequently used for historical research and for preservation and restoration purposes.

Civil War cartographers were involved in reconnaissance, pre-battle, and post-battle mapping. oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:title: Henry, a slave v. State (1850) Franklin map exhibit
oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:description: Hand-drawn map of Franklin accompanying the 1850 Supreme Court case file of Henry, a slave v. State of Tennessee. The map exhibit details the area where Main Street and Columbia Turnpike intersect. Many churches, businesses, and homes are depicted as are the locations that the bodies of Barham and Eelbeck were found. The Presbyterian Church, an Episcopal Church [St. Paul's], female institute [Franklin Female Institute], and a male academy [Harpeth Academy] are all denoted. Businesses include Boyd's Store, McGan's shop, and a tanyard. Homeowners include Hannah Henderson [where the local enslaved population held prayer meetings], Baugh, Betsy Wills, McGan, Wells, Courtney, McConnell, Park, Dr. Ewing, Bennett, Bridge, and Harrison.

Henry, enslaved by John D. Bennett, was accused of the murders of John G. Eelbeck and William Barham on the night of February 24, 1850. Eelbeck was stabbed in the left breast with a knife and sustained a wound two inches wide, and three inches deep. After a grand jury indictment, Henry, through court appointed attorneys, pled not guilty. On November 26, 1850, the jury found Henry guilty and sentenced him to be hanged on December 14. During testimony, Dr. A. B. Ewing described Eelbeck as a 22 year old white male, weighing about 120 pounds. Ewing and other witnesses described Henry as stout and sporting a long goatee. Witnesses mentioned seeing Henry with a butcher knife earlier in the day, some identified Henry as the murderer, while others refused to identify him as such. Another man, William P. Barham, was killed in the scuffle the three had near the corner of Columbia Turnpike, Margin St., and Main St. The appeal made it to the Tennessee Supreme Court where the lower court judgement was affirmed. Henry Bennett was hanged on February 21, 1851. Many witnesses in the case were enslaved persons, they are all named and their owners indicated.

oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:description: Detailed view of the neighborhoods north of the capitol, including parts of Hell’s Half Acre, Smokey Row, and Germantown. The old street names are visible as are the various additions to the city of Nashville. The Lick Branch was still above ground and runs through the area depicted in this plate. A Louisville and Nashville (L&N) Railyard is located in the bottom right of the plate, next door to the Linck's Hotel. Various school buildings, churches, and businesses populate the lots and some landowners are named. The blocks along the river were industrial, containing saw mills, ice factories, stock yards, a gas works, tannery, and other large manufactories and businesses. The city owns some of the land toward the center. An early grandstand is seen at Sulphur Dell, but is unnamed until the 1908 version of Hopkins Atlas. A legend is located in the bottom right.

Griffith Morgan Hopkins was born around 1836, however the exact date is unknown. He first began printing maps in 1857 and continued until his retirement in 1900. He founded G. M. Hopkins & Co. with his brother Henry W. Hopkins, and together they produced many city and county atlases, primarily of the northeast, from their shop in Philadelphia. Their 1908 Atlas of Nashville is a fine, block-by-block depiction of the town in a period of growth to a modern urban center. G. M. Hopkins & Co. continued on after the founders' retirements until the Great Depression ended the demand for their atlases. The company was sold to the Franklin Survey Company in 1943, with the name intact, due to its association with quality.

Susan Cannon Glasgow Haywood married Thomas Jefferson Haywood, son of Judge John Haywood. John Haywood purchased the land from James Lynch. He apparently paid for the land with credit and at the time of his death still owed on it. The land went up for auction and defendant Ensley bought it, supposedly with the understanding that nobody would bid against him because he was purchasing the land for the benefit of plaintiffs. Ensley claimed to have won over two other bidders. The chancellor ultimately sided with Ensley and ruled that Haywood must repay the purchase amount if he were to take possession of the land. On January 1, 1812, Willie Blount leased this plot of land to a John Den (a 19th century form of John Doe) to farm for ten years. John Den, the unnamed lessee, accused a Richard Fen (another 19th century form of John Doe) of forcibly coming onto the land, "wrong[ed]" him and did five hundred dollars worth of damage. At some point in the case the charge of ejectment was added to the original bill, the addition of which created a constitutionality issue. oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:description: This map shows the movements of Union and Confederate troop positions during the Battle of Franklin on November 30, 1864. Union movements are in blue and Confederate movements are in red. Battlefield landmarks and home are indicated including bridges, fords, the toll gate, the saw mill, roads, and railroads. Relief shown by hachures.

The Battle of Franklin was one of the worst disasters of the Civil War for the Confederate Army. Confederate Lt. Gen. John Bell Hood's Army of Tennessee conducted numerous frontal assaults against Union forces under Maj. Gen. John M. Schofield and was unable to break through. The Confederates ultimately took Franklin, but at great cost, incurring over six thousand casualties including fourteen generals.

The Battle of Gettysburg, often regarded as the turning point of the Civil War, was fought July 1 to July 3, 1863. Buoyed by his success at Chancellorsville, Lee hoped to shift the mood of northern politicians and citizens alike with an invasion into Pennsylvania. Lee's Army of Northern VIrginia met Meade's Army of the Potomac near the town of Gettysburg. The battle resulted in the greatest number of casualties of the Civil War, some 23,000 on each side. oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:title: Movements of Gen. T. J. "Stonewall" Jackson, 1861-1863
oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:description: Map of the military movements of Thomas Jonathan "Stonewall" Jackson during the American Civil War. Depicts his route during the war along with the dates of his movements and battles in which he fought, and the route his body took from the time of his death until burial. The map is published compliments of Stonewall Jackson Memorial, Inc.,

Thomas Jonathan "Stonewall" Jackson was born on January 21, 1824 in Clarksburg, Virginia [West Virginia]. Jackson was accepted to United States Military Academy and graduated in 1846. He fought in the Mexican-American War, eventually gaining a brevet promotion to major. Following the war, he taught at the Virginia Military Institute until the outbreak of the Civil War. He was promoted to brigadier general by the end of June 1861 and earned his famous nickname at the First Battle of Bull Run on July 21, 1861. He was promoted to major general in October 1861, and given command of the Valley District where he earned fame and popularity in the South for his military success. After the Second Battle of Bull Run and Antietam, Jackson was promoted to lieutenant general, and was outranked only by Lee and Longstreet. At the Battle of Chancellorsville, he led a flanking maneuver that devastated the Union's right side. Jackson was shot by Confederate patrols upon returning to camp the night of the assault, May 2, and died eight days later from pneumonia on May 10, 1863.

oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:description: Plat of land around the Tennessee State Capitol during the final phases of construction. It shows property lines, lot widths, and landowners. High Street, Vine Street, Cedar Street, and Gay Street are named. A handwritten note to the left states "Mr. Plunkett wants you to draw a plat of all the Capitol ground and the different lots adjoining it," possibly signed by James S. Young.

The lot designated as Hospital was the site of Tennessee's first Catholic Church, built in 1820 by Irish Catholic bridgebuilders. In 1830, the parishioners replaced the frame church with a brick building and designated it Holy Rosary Cathedral. The construction of St. Mary's Cathedral on 5th made the small cathedral obsolete and in 1847, it became St. John's Hospital and Orphanage. The plot was sold to the state in 1857 during the finishing stages of the capitol's construction. The Capitol Building Commission authorized the following amounts to purchase adjoining lots: Martin - $6000, Spain - $2250, Wynn - $7000, Torbett - $2000, Freeman - $6000, and Crockett -$2400.

oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:title: Gulf Stream and drifts
oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:description: Current chart of the Atlantic Ocean drawn by Matthew Fontaine Maury for his book The Physical Geography of the Sea. The coasts of North America, South America, Africa, and Spain are included. Particular attention and detail is given to the Gulf Stream which includes annotations. Also included are the Great Equatorial Current, a forest of seaweed, and the Sargasso Sea, the confluence of the four major Atlantic sea currents.

Matthew Fontaine Maury was born in Spotsylvania County, Virginia in 1806. His parents moved to Franklin, Tennessee in 1811. With the help of family friend Sam Houston, Maury joined the Navy as a midshipman aboard the Brandywine. After breaking his right leg in a stagecoach accident, Maury focused on studying navigation, naval meteorology, and oceanography. His work, The Physical Geography of the Sea, was the first comprehensive study on oceanography and earned him the nickname the "Father of Modern Oceanography." At the outbreak of the Civil War, Maury joined the Confederacy, serving as Chief of Sea Coast, River, and Harbor Defenses. One of his primary missions was to spread Confederate propaganda and purchase ships. After the war, Maury taught at Virginia Military Institute. He died on February 1, 1873 at his home in Lexington, Virginia. John Meigs, the first assistant State Librarian, obtained this book directly from Maury in 1857.

oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:description: Hand-drawn map of land in Prince William County, Virginia, (present-day Quantico) along the Potomac River from September 1861. The map shows Confederate troop placements, with named regiments, camps, and batteries. The location of the brigade commissary and magazines are specified. Quantico and Chopawamsic creeks are drawn and annotated. Local landowners and their residences are denoted as are various roads, creeks, and mills. The towns of Dumfries and Evansport are included. Relief shown by hachures.

W. W. Fergusson was born in Smith County in 1831 to Adam and Hester Fergusson. He studied law at Cumberland College in Lebanon. At the outbreak of the Civil War, Fergusson volunteered for the Confederate Army and was attached to the 2nd Tennessee, as a topographical engineer, under Colonel William B. Bate. After participation at the First Battle of Bull Run, the unit was transferred under Col. J. G. Walker and they moved to Evansport to erect batteries along the Potomac. In February 1862, he was ordered to Knoxville to help construct defenses, and after the fall of Forts Donelson and Henry, rendezvoused with the Army of Mississippi to meet the Union at Shiloh. Fergusson went on to participate in the Chattanooga and Atlanta campaigns and surrendered with the Army of Tennessee at Greensboro, North Carolina in 1865. After the war, Fergusson opened Blackgnat Academy in Riddleton, practiced law, and married Medora Kerby, with whom he had eight children. Fergusson died in 1922.

oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:description: This map covers parts of Arizona, New Mexico, Texas, and Mexico. Geographic features include springs, creeks, rivers, lakes, and mountain ranges.

The Chiricahua are a band of Apache that lived in the area depicted by the map. Following the Mexican-American War and Gadsden Purchase, the influx of Americans to their homeland accelerated, exacerbating tensions. From 1861 until 1886, the Apache Wars ravaged the Southwest United States. On top of growing tensions, the US Army killed some of Cochise's relatives in 1861, an event known as the Bascom Affair. Cochise, a principal chief of a band of the Chiricahua Apache, waged a guerilla war to avenge his relatives' deaths. After a decade of fighting, the Chiricahua signed a peace treaty with the United States which created a reservation in present-day New Mexico and Arizona. Cochise died of natural causes in 1874. Many Chiricahua found life in their new desert home difficult and began leaving. Under a popular resistance leader, Geronimo, they occasionally raided nearby settlements until their surrender to General Nelson A. Miles in 1886.

oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:title: The Republic of Texas, 1836
oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:description: This colorful map shows the early boundaries of the Republic of Texas in 1836. Rivers, mountains, and emigration trails are shown. The Santa Fe Trail is on the map along with illustrations of settlers traveling along it in covered wagons. In the center, Native Americans (the Comanches were near this area) are chasing buffalo. The text details the boundaries of Texas and the Declaration of Independence from Mexico. During James K. Polk's presidency, the nation expanded significantly with the annexation of the Republic of Texas.

During the presidential election of 1844, the annexation of Texas and the expansion of slavery was a major issue. The Whig Party nominee, Henry Clay, adopted an anti-annexation platform on the principle of preserving the North-South sectional unity and to avoid war by respecting Mexico's claims to Texas. The Democrats nominated James K. Polk who ran on a platform that embraced America's popular commitment to territorial expansion, often referred to as Manifest Destiny. During the presidential campaign, Polk successfully linked the United States-British boundary dispute over the partition of Oregon Territory with the Texas annexation debate. By doing so, Polk united the anti-slavery Northern expansionists, who demanded Oregon as free from slavery with pro-slavery Southern expansionists, who insisted on acquiring Texas as a slave state. After a hard fought campaign, James K. Polk was elected as the eleventh president of the United States. Eventually, Texas was annexed and became part of the United States on December 29, 1845.

James H. Simpson was born in New Brunswick, New Jersey, in 1813. He graduated from West Point in 1832, assigned to the 3rd U.S. Artillery. After serving in the Second Seminole War, Simpson joined the topographical engineers. He surveyed for the New Mexico Expedition in 1849 and the Utah Expedition in 1858 to 1859. At the outbreak of the Civil War, Simpson joined the 4th New Jersey Volunteer Infantry and was captured at the Battle of Gaines's Mill. He was paroled, returned to the topographical engineers and joined the Department of the Ohio. After the war, Simpson was appointed chief engineer of the Interior Department and supervised the laying of the Transcontinental Railroad. He died March 2, 1883.

Washington County is Tennessee's oldest county, organizing itself as the Washington District in the early 1770s until it was annexed by North Carolina and officially dubbed Washington County in 1777. It was a part of the failed State of Franklin in the 1780s, and the territory south of the River Ohio in the 1790s, before ultimately joining Tennessee after admittance to the Union in 1796. It is named for General and President George Washington. Its county seat is Jonesborough, named for North Carolina statesman Willie Jones, while its largest city is Johnson City, is named for an early settler, Henry Johnson. Johnson City briefly changed its name to Haynesville during the Civil War to honor Confederate senator Landon Carter Haynes.

oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:description: This color map, compiled by the Bureau of Indian Affairs, identifies military stations and Indian agencies in the United States and territories in the 1880s. Inset maps of Alaska, Mission Indian Reservation of California, and Indian Territory are included.

By the 1840s, thousands of American Indians had been forced from their homelands and pushed West to Indian Territory in present-day Oklahoma. In the late 1880s, after these displaced civilizations were finally prospering in their new home, the United States government halved Indian Territory, opening the remainder for white settlers. Once Oklahoma became a state in 1907, the remaining American Indians lost their sovereignty. Many served in World War II, notably the Navajo Code Talkers, but returned to more hardship implemented by the federal government. Federal agents would remove native children from their families to raise them under the state's protection, eliminating familial and cultural ties. It wasn't until the 1970s that American Indians began to exert political influence nationally.

oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:description: This plate depicts an area of Nashville just north of the Cumberland River and east of Russell St. in present-day East Nashville. Most of this area was once owned by Dr. John Shelby noted in the many city additions and road that bear his name as well as his expansive estate near the bottom of the plate.

Griffith Morgan Hopkins was born around 1836, however the exact date is unknown. He first began printing maps in 1857 and continued until his retirement in 1900. He founded G. M. Hopkins & Co. with his brother Henry W. Hopkins, and together they produced many city and county atlases, primarily of the northeast, from their shop in Philadelphia. Their 1908 Atlas of Nashville is a fine, block-by-block depiction of the town in a period of growth to a modern urban center. G. M. Hopkins & Co. continued on after the founders' retirements until the Great Depression ended the demand for their atlases. The company was sold to the Franklin Survey Company in 1943, with the name intact, due to its association with quality.

Daniel Alfred Sanborn, a civil engineer and surveyor, began working on fire insurance maps in the 1860s and his company soon became one of the largest and most successful American map companies. Sanborn's first work mapping cities for insurance purposes began in Tennessee when Aetna Insurance hired him to survey a few towns across the state, however none of these earliest examples are known to exist today (Ristow, Walter W. "United States Fire Insurance and Underwriters Maps· 1852—1968." The Quarterly Journal of the Library of Congress 25, no. 3 (1968): 194-218." Sanborn maps were originally created to estimate fire insurance risks. Insurance companies would decide how much insurance, if any, was to be offered to a customer solely through the use of a Sanborn map. Today, the maps are frequently used for historical research and for preservation and restoration purposes.

oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:title: James County, Tennessee
oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:description: This hand-drawn map shows the boundary lines for James County in 1871, the year the county was officially established. The town of Ooltewah (the county seat) is shown, as are Chattanooga and Cleveland situated beyond the boundaries. The total area for James County was approximately 330 square miles.

Predominantly white, rural, and poor, James County arose out of the political factionalism of the Reconstruction Era. In 1871, Representative Elbert A. James, a Democrat from Hamilton County, introduced legislation for the formation of the county, named in honor of his father, Rev. Jesse J. James. The elder James, a Methodist minister from Sullivan County, first moved to Chattanooga in the 1850s. Three days after Rep. James introduced his bill, the Tennessee General Assembly passed the act creating James County on Jan. 30, 1871. Lawmakers chose Ooltewah as the county seat, and subsequently citizens began work on building a county courthouse. Following 19 years of meager existence, state lawmakers passed an act on March 11, 1890 abolishing the county and returning the land to the parent counties of Hamilton and Bradley.

oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:description: Plate 9 of the 1889 Atlas of Nashville detailing the area near Vanderbilt University. The school's campus is shown including Wesley Hall, Science Hall, the chancellor's residence, the president's house, various dormitories, and the gymnasium. The large estate of Samuel M. Murphy, whom the Davidson County trustee listed as the second wealthiest Nashvillian in 1897, is seen just north of Vanderbilt. The old State Fairgrounds, now called West Side Park and later Centennial Park after Nashville's Centennial Exposition was held there in 1897, is included. Various other tracts and additions to the city are drawn.

Griffith Morgan Hopkins was born around 1836, however the exact date is unknown. He first began printing maps in 1857 and continued until his retirement in 1900. He founded G. M. Hopkins & Co. with his brother Henry W. Hopkins, and together they produced many city and county atlases, primarily of the northeast, from their shop in Philadelphia. Their 1908 Atlas of Nashville is a fine, block-by-block depiction of the town in a period of growth to a modern urban center. G. M. Hopkins & Co. continued on after the founders' retirements until the Great Depression ended the demand for their atlases. The company was sold to the Franklin Survey Company in 1943, with the name intact, due to its association with quality.

After America's first settlers crossed the Bering land bridge into North America, the Pacific Northwest became their earliest home within the present boundaries of the contiguous United States. The first Europeans arrived by sea in the 18th century until the famous Lewis and Clark Expedition reached Washington in 1805. Following the Oregon boundary dispute, the US/Canada border was established as the 49th parallel. Thereafter, the Oregon Territory was created in 1848. Washington Territory was established in 1853 from the northern portion of the Oregon Territory and existed until Washington became the 42nd state in 1889. A number of American Indian tribes remain in Washington on over 3 million acres of federally administered reservations.

oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:title: The Silurian Basin of Middle Tennessee
oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:description: This map, published in the Southern Journal of Medical and Physical Sciences, depicts Middle Tennessee's basin in geological terms. Cities rivers, cedar glades, barrens, and mountains are drawn. A key outlining the various geologic periods noted across the basin is at the bottom left. A cross section of the basin appears to the right of the map nearly into the book's binding. Relief shown by hachures.

The Silurian Basin refers to the Silurian geologic period the lasted from 443.8 million years ago until 419.2 million years ago, noted for its distinct rock beds. The beginning of the Silurian period is marked by a major extinction event that killed 60% of all marine life. The Silurian period is also when bony fish began to flourish in Earth's oceans and the first multicellular life began on land.

Edward Barnwell Heyward was born in 1826 to Charles Heyward and Emma Barnwell Heyward. The senior Heyward owned four, primarily rice, plantations in South Carolina. Edward graduated from South Carolina College in 1845 and shortly thereafter embarked on a Grand Tour of Europe, which this map's markings document. E. B. served the Confederacy during the Civil War as an engineer. Following the war, 491 enslaved people were emancipated from various Heyward plantations, many of which burned during the war. Heyward died in 1871. His son, Duncan Clinch Heyward, served as Governor of South Carolina from 1903-1907. (www.lowcountryafricana.com/south-caroliniana-library-at-usc/) and (Stroup, Rodger E. Before and after: Three letters from E. B. Heyward." The second copy of this map was purchased by Charles Izard Manigault, a cousin of E. B. Heyward, in Paris, while on a Grand Tour from 1847 to 1848. A letterbook from his stay in Paris resides at the South Carolina Historical Society.

The Nashville and Northwestern Railroad was chartered in 1852. By the outbreak of the Civil War, the tracks connected Nashville with Kingston Springs, TN, and HIckman, KY with McKenzie, TN. Once the Union Army captured Nashville and the railroad, they impressed formerly enslaved African Americans to extend it westward from Kingston Springs to Johnsonville. In April 1868, funding for workers ran dry and in June the workers went on strike to protest their lack of pay. In 1872, the Nashville and Chattanooga Railroad purchased the Nashville and Northwestern and reincorporated under the name Nashville, Chattanooga, and St. Louis Railway.

William A. Eichbaum was born in Dublin, Ireland in April 1787. His father was a German immigrant, who worked in Ireland as a glass maker. William immigrated to America around 1820, after a brief journey to Peru. In 1825, he married Catharine M. Stearns, a teacher at Nashville Female Academy. Eichbaum became one of Nashville's foremost booksellers in the mid-19th century. He participated in many philanthropic and societal organizations including the Davidson County Bible Society, Horticultural Society, Nashville Historical Society, Mount Olivet Cemetery Company, and Nashville Savings Company. Daniel Alfred Sanborn, a civil engineer and surveyor, began working on fire insurance maps in the 1860s and his company soon became one of the largest and most successful American map companies. Sanborn's first work mapping cities for insurance purposes began in Tennessee when Aetna Insurance hired him to survey a few towns across the state, however none of these earliest examples are known to exist today (Ristow, Walter W. "United States Fire Insurance and Underwriters Maps· 1852—1968." The Quarterly Journal of the Library of Congress 25, no. 3 (1968): 194-218." Sanborn maps were originally created to estimate fire insurance risks. Insurance companies would decide how much insurance, if any, was to be offered to a customer solely through the use of a Sanborn map. Today, the maps are frequently used for historical research and for preservation and restoration purposes.

oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:description: Map of a portion of Alabama from Albert James Pickett's History of Alabama, 3rd edition, 1851. The Creek War (1813-1814) was a sub-conflict of the War of 1812, but for most Tennesseans the Creek War was the War of 1812. With the noticeable exception of the campaign at New Orleans, the battles fought in the Creek conflict represented the majority of fighting by Tennessee troops. Most Tennessee deaths and casualties occurred during the Creek War. Iconic figures such as Sam Houston and David Crockett fought the Red Sticks, the warring faction of the Creek Nation, although neither man had yet to achieve any fame. The Creek War established Andrew Jackson as a household name, and his victories prompted officials in Washington to promote him to major general in the U.S. Army. This promotion placed him in command at New Orleans and set him on a road to immortal fame. The land seized from the Creek following the war began the final era of land cessions in the southeast that culminated in forced removal in the 1830s.

Griffith Morgan Hopkins was born around 1836, however the exact date is unknown. He first began printing maps in 1857 and continued until his retirement in 1900. He founded G. M. Hopkins & Co. with his brother Henry W. Hopkins, and together they produced many city and county atlases, primarily of the northeast, from their shop in Philadelphia. Their 1908 Atlas of Nashville is a fine, block-by-block depiction of the town in a period of growth to a modern urban center. G. M. oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:title: Sanborn Fire Insurance Map of Memphis, Tenn. (1897, rev. 1911)
oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:description: Plates 151-152 of the 1911 revision of the Sanborn Fire Insurance Atlas of Memphis. This neighborhood was in the midst of a change from a white middle class neighborhood to a black middle class neighborhood and business district, evidenced by the "negro tenements" and black churches, including Centenary Methodist Episcopal and Metropolitan Baptist Church. The area on plate 152 was razed in 1939 for the construction of William H. Foote Homes, a public housing project.

Daniel Alfred Sanborn, a civil engineer and surveyor, began working on fire insurance maps in the 1860s and his company soon became one of the largest and most successful American map companies. Sanborn's first work mapping cities for insurance purposes began in Tennessee when Aetna Insurance hired him to survey a few towns across the state, however none of these earliest examples are known to exist today (Ristow, Walter W. "United States Fire Insurance and Underwriters Maps· 1852—1968." The Quarterly Journal of the Library of Congress 25, no. 3 (1968): 194-218." Sanborn maps were originally created to estimate fire insurance risks. Insurance companies would decide how much insurance, if any, was to be offered to a customer solely through the use of a Sanborn map. Today, the maps are frequently used for historical research and for preservation and restoration purposes.

TSLA holds a large collection of these WWII "newsmaps" detailing for the American public the weekly events of US military efforts in Europe and the Pacific theaters. The Bureau of Public Relations was established in the Office of the Secretary of War in February 1941. The Bureau served as the central War Department agency to determine policies and procedures for disseminating military information to the public. After August 1942, it was also responsible for the public relations activities of the Army Air Forces, the Army Service Forces and the Army Ground Forces. During the war, the Bureau produced these weekly newsmaps for War Department distribution.

oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:title: Geological map of Tennessee
oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:description: A color-coded geological map of Tennessee showing rock formations, commercial deposits and mines, and iron-making operations across the state. Executed by James Safford, Tennessee's state geologist, it details the locations of mineral deposits, iron furnaces, forges and bloomeries, mills, coal mines, and marble quarries. Along the bottom is a geological cross section of the state with a rough elevation projection. Same as Map 366A in the TSLA Map Collection.

James M. Safford was a chemist, geologist, and professor in Tennessee. He studied chemistry at Yale, and taught geology, chemistry, and botany at the University of Nashville, Cumberland University, and Vanderbilt University. He served as State Geologist for the much of the latter half of the 19th century, and his geological survey of Tennessee in 1869 is still cited in the field today. He and J. B. Killebrew published a report on the agricultural and mineral resources of Tennessee which served as the basis for textbooks, pamphlets, essays, and bulletins for decades thereafter.

oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:title: Tennessee colored state normal and industrial school plat map
oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:description: Plat map of the Riverside subdivision adjacent to the Tennessee Agricultural and Industrial State Normal School. Hand-drawn notes indicate ownership information of some of the lots, however it is unknown who drew them. On school lands are images of three original school buildings now demolished: the male dormitory, the female dormitory, and the main building. A bird's-eye view of the undeveloped property south of the school spans the bottom.

The Tennessee General Assembly created the Tennessee Agricultural and Industrial State Normal School in 1909, but the school officially opened in 1912. In 1944, the school graduated its first master's students. In 1951 the school officially became a university. The school changed its named to Tennessee State University in 1968 and currently maintains two campuses in Nashville. It is the only public Historically Black College and University (HBCU) in Tennessee. Many of the lots sold by Riverview Realty Company were purchased by African Americans at auction on June 28, 1912.

oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:title: Battlefield of Chattanooga with the operations of the national forces under the command of Maj. Gen. U.S. Grant during the battles of Nov. 23, 24, & 25, 1863
oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:description: Indicates troop positions, Union and Confederate headquarters, roads, railroads, drainage, vegetation, relief by shading, and the names of a few residents in the outlying areas.

Following their victory at the Battle of Chickamauga, General Braxton Bragg’s Army of Tennessee chased Union forces under Major General William Rosecrans to Chattanooga. The Union settled behind the defenses in the city, while the Confederates occupied the surrounding high ground. Major General Ulysses S. Grant was given command of Federal forces in the western theater, and was joined with reinforcements. On October 27, the Union were able to open a “Cracker Line” at Brown’s Ferry to resupply their troops. After small battles at Wauhatchie and Orchard Knob, Major General Joseph Hooker launched an assault, overrunning Confederate positions on Lookout Mountain on November 24th, just in time to assist Grant’s advance on Bragg’s position at Missionary Ridge. The result was a resounding victory for the Union, crushing the Confederates' hopes that emerged from their victory at Chickamauga. Chattanooga became the supply center for General William T. Sherman’s Atlanta Campaign.
oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:creator: Smith, W. F.

oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:title: Map of the state of Florida (1856)
oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:description: Highly detailed map of Florida made by the Bureau of Topographical Engineers. It shows the township and range grid, roads, railroads, canals, cities, forts, and counties. Geographic features include rivers, lakes, islands, marshes, swamps, lagoons, capes, inlets, and oceans. The map indicates various unexplored areas of the state. The Everglades are shown by hachure.

This map was "donated to the Tennessee Historical Society by the Hon. John Bell in 1859." John Bell was born in Nashville in 1796. In 1814, he graduated from Cumberland College and studied law until his admittance to the bar in 1816. He served in the State Senate, U. S. House of Representatives, and U. S. Senate. During Bell's tenure in the U. S. House, he drafted the the Indian Removal Act. However, the Bank Wars caused a rift between Bell and his old friend Andrew Jackson. He was elected Speaker of the U. S. House of Representatives as an anti-Jacksonian in 1834. In 1841, William Henry Harrison selected Bell as his Secretary of War, rewarding him for his support of Harrison's presidential campaign. Following his tenure in the Senate, Bell ran for president under the Constitutional Union party, narrowly defeating Samuel Houston for the party's nomination. He received nearly 600,000 popular votes and 39 electoral votes, from Virginia, Kentucky, and Tennessee. Initially supporting the Union, Bell defected to the Confederacy following the Union's invasion of Tennessee. He died at his home near Dover, Tennessee, in 1869.

oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:title: Battlefield in front of Franklin, Tenn.
oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:description: Map shows Battle of Franklin where the United States Forces repulsed the Confederate Army on November 30, 1864. Includes topography, roads, disposition of Union works and Confederate forces, houses and landowners, fortified positions, and layout of Town of Franklin. Blueprint version of Map 27 in the TSLA Map Collection.

The Battle of Franklin was one of the worst disasters of the Civil War for the Confederate Army. Confederate Lt. Gen. John Bell Hood's Army of Tennessee conducted numerous frontal assaults against Union forces under Maj. Gen. John M. Schofield and was unable to break through. The Confederates ultimately took Franklin, but at great cost, incurring over six thousand casualties including fourteen generals. Though published ten years after the battle, this map contains a wealth of important details and was compiled by Col. William E. Merrill, one of the foremost Union cartographers working in Tennessee during the Civil War.

oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:title: Map of Indian Territory and Oklahoma
oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:description: Map of the Indian Territory showing tribal boundaries, roads, railroads, cities, towns, missions, schools, treaty dates, rivers, and creeks.Relief shown by hachures. Taken from the 1890 census.

By the 1840s, thousands of American Indians had been forced from their homelands and pushed West to Indian Territory in present-day Oklahoma. In the late 1880s, after these displaced civilizations were finally prospering in their new home, the United States government halved Indian Territory, opening the remainder for white settlers. Once Oklahoma became a state in 1907, the remaining American Indians lost their sovereignty. Many served in World War II, notably the Navajo Code Talkers, but returned to more hardship implemented by the federal government. Federal agents would remove native children from their families to raise them under the state's protection, eliminating familial and cultural ties. It wasn't until the 1970s that American Indians began to exert political influence nationally.

oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:title: Nashville. Plate 2 from G. M. Hopkins' Atlas of Nashville (1889)
oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:description: Plate 2 depicts downtown Nashville between Union and Broad streets. Many churches, including First Presbyterian and the non-extant Vine Street Temple, are shown. Businesses include theaters, hotels, foundries, iron and soep works, banks, and many other unnamed proprietorships. Educational institutions include University of Tennessee Medical and Dental Departments, Watkins Institute, and the Tennessee Historical Society. A number of property owners are identified.

Griffith Morgan Hopkins was born around 1836, however the exact date is unknown. He first began printing maps in 1857 and continued until his retirement in 1900. He founded G. M. Hopkins & Co. with his brother Henry W. Hopkins, and together they produced many city and county atlases, primarily of the northeast, from their shop in Philadelphia. Their 1908 Atlas of Nashville is a fine, block-by-block depiction of the town in a period of growth to a modern urban center. G. M. Hopkins & Co. continued on after the founders' retirements until the Great Depression ended the demand for their atlases. The company was sold to the Franklin Survey Company in 1943, with the name intact, due to its association with quality.

oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:title: [Index Map] Sanborn Fire Insurance Map of Nashville, Tenn. (1897, rev. 1911)
oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:description: Index map to Volume 1 of the 1897 edition of the Sanborn Fire Insurance Atlas of Nashville. Plates 1-99 are identified, encompassing most of the area of downtown Nashville north of Broad Street. A street index is included on the left-hand page.

Daniel Alfred Sanborn, a civil engineer and surveyor, began working on fire insurance maps in the 1860s and his company soon became one of the largest and most successful American map companies. Sanborn's first work mapping cities for insurance purposes began in Tennessee when Aetna Insurance hired him to survey a few towns across the state, however none of these earliest examples are known to exist today (Ristow, Walter W. "United States Fire Insurance and Underwriters Maps· 1852—1968." The Quarterly Journal of the Library of Congress 25, no. 3 (1968): 194-218." Sanborn maps were originally created to estimate fire insurance risks. Insurance companies would decide how much insurance, if any, was to be offered to a customer solely through the use of a Sanborn map. Today, the maps are frequently used for historical research and for preservation and restoration purposes.

Verso shows Chinese soldiers with text translating common Chinese phrases and describing some Chinese culture and history.

TSLA holds a large collection of these WWII "newsmaps" detailing for the American public the weekly events of US military efforts in Europe and the Pacific theaters. The Bureau of Public Relations was established in the Office of the Secretary of War in February 1941. The Bureau served as the central War Department agency to determine policies and procedures for disseminating military information to the public. After August 1942, it was also responsible for the public relations activities of the Army Air Forces, the Army Service Forces and the Army Ground Forces. During the war, the Bureau produced these weekly newsmaps for War Department distribution.

oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:title: Town of Port Royal
oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:description: Microfilm copy of an 1836 deed book showing a plat of the small town of Port Royal, Tennessee on the Red River. Public square, streets and town lots are all denoted.

Port Royal is one of the earliest white settlements in Middle Tennessee. Incorporated in 1797, its position at the confluence of important upper MIddle Tennessee waterways saw it become an important regional commercial center. Because of this, one of Tennessee's most important stagecoach roads ran through Port Royal. The road, used by the Cherokee forced from their homeland on the Trail of Tears, crossed the Red River at Port Royal. The Civil War brought economic collapse to the South and when the railroad skipped Port Royal, its days as an important economic center were over. Its historic importance led to the creation of Port Royal State Park, which contains the town.

oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:title: John C. Ferris, admr of Wiley D. Snyder vs. the Nashville & Chattanooga Railroad et al (1872) map exhibit
oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:description: A Nashville street map, hand-drawn in ink and pencil on architectural fabric. Depicts the Nashville & Chattanooga Railroad line where it crossed under Broad Street and McGavock Street; the tunnel above which is labeled Lawrence Street. Also depicted is Demumbrane (Demonbreun) Street, Vauxhall Street, Gowdey Street, and Granny White Pike. The homes and structures indicated on the map are the Oil Works, Snyder’s House, Prichett’s House, Mrs. Pyles, a Negro Cabin, a Brickhouse, and Fanny Thompson’s house. Also indicated is the location in which Snyder was killed, and the name McCall.

This map was used as evidence in a Tennessee Supreme Court case brought against the Nashville & Chattanooga R.R. by the widow of Wiley D. Snyder. Snyder was mortally injured when he either fell or was thrown into a deep railroad cut near Demonbreun Street and Granny White Pike. The plaintiff in the case alleged the defendant was legally responsible for Snyder’s injuries and subsequent death due to the danger posed by the open railroad cut. The defense alleged that Snyder’s accident was due to his own negligence or may have been precipitated by a physical assault on Snyder by a person or persons unknown. Judgment rendered in favor of the defendant.

oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:title: Wind and current chart of the North Atlantic
oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:description: Series D, Sheet 1 of Matthew Fontaine Maury's hydrographic charts depicting surface temperatures of the ocean in the Gulf of Mexico and the Atlantic Ocean off the Eastern seaboard of the United States.

Matthew Fontaine Maury was born in Spotsylvania County, Virginia in 1806. His parents moved to Franklin, Tennessee in 1811. With the help of family friend Sam Houston, Maury joined the Navy as a midshipman aboard the Brandywine. After breaking his right leg in a stagecoach accident, Maury focused on studying navigation, naval meteorology, and oceanography. His work, The Physical Geography of the Sea, was the first comprehensive study on oceanography and earned him the nickname the "Father of Modern Oceanography." At the outbreak of the Civil War, Maury joined the Confederacy, serving as Chief of Sea Coast, River, and Harbor Defenses. One of his primary missions was to spread Confederate propaganda and purchase ships. After the war, Maury taught at Virginia Military Institute. He died on February 1, 1873 at his home in Lexington, Virginia.

David H. Burr was born in Bridgeport Connecticut, in 1803. After attending law school, Burr embarked on a career as a cartographer and surveyor. His 1829 Atlas of the State of New York, was only the second state atlas produced in America, following Robert Mills' 1825 Atlas of South Carolina. Burr was paid $2358.88 for his efforts and produced this magnificent atlas complete with hand-colored maps. Copies of the atlas were sent to the governor of each state to showcase New York's grandeur. The copy is one of his first editions with numerous later editions published by Burr himself, as well as J. H. Colton, who purchased Burr's printing plates in 1833. This atlas served as the source of later New York state and county maps until at least the 1870s. (Mano, Jo Margaret. Mapping the County: Burr's New York State Atlas)

His World War I draft registration describes him as a short and slender man with black eyes and graying hair. On August 3, 1900, he and Daisy Andrews married in Putnam County. At the time of this marriage, A. P. lived at home and worked as a grain dealer. Before he launched A. P. Welch and Company he worked as a minister, farmer, and for Cookeville Veneer Company. His business, A. P. Welch and Company, bought and sold lumber, coal, real estate, and feed. Under this styling, Welch served as the purchasing agent for Carthage Spoke and Cooperage Company and Cookeville Veneer Company. He served as a director of The Welch Stave and Heading Company with his relatives George Nathaniel Welch, John W. Welch, J. P. Welch, and J. N. Welch. A. P. helped found Monterey Nazarene Church in 1903 and continued preaching full-time until 1930. A. P. and Daisy Welch had three daughters, Lucile, Margaret Josephine, and Ruth. He died on January 9, 1956, and is buried in Welch Memorial Cemetery in Putnam County.

oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:title: Plate 553. Sanborn Fire Insurance Map of Nashville, Tenn.
oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:description: Plate 553 of a the 1920 Sanborn Fire Insurance Atlas of Nashville. This loose sheet is part of a set of unadulterated 1920 Sanborn plates of Nashville. It depicts Tennessee Agricultural and Industrial School (A&I), later renamed Tennessee State University (TSU). Another section shows the Read Phosphate Company plant outside Nashville.

Daniel Alfred Sanborn, a civil engineer and surveyor, began working on fire insurance maps in the 1860s and his company soon became one of the largest and most successful American map companies. Sanborn's first work mapping cities for insurance purposes began in Tennessee when Aetna Insurance hired him to survey a few towns across the state, however none of these earliest examples are known to exist today (Ristow, Walter W. "United States Fire Insurance and Underwriters Maps· 1852—1968." The Quarterly Journal of the Library of Congress 25, no. 3 (1968): 194-218.). Sanborn maps were originally created to estimate fire insurance risks. Insurance companies would decide how much insurance, if any, was to be offered to a customer solely through the use of a Sanborn map. Today, the maps are frequently used for historical research and for preservation and restoration purposes.

Rhea County was formed in 1807 from Roane County, and was split to form Meigs County in 1836. It is named for Revolutionary War veteran and Tennessee statesman, John Rhea. Griffith Morgan Hopkins was born around 1836, however the exact date is unknown. He first began printing maps in 1857 and continued until his retirement in 1900. He founded G. M. Hopkins & Co. with his brother Henry W. Hopkins, and together they produced many city and county atlases, primarily of the northeast, from their shop in Philadelphia. Their 1908 Atlas of Nashville is a fine, block-by-block depiction of the town in a period of growth to a modern urban center. G. M. Hopkins & Co. continued on after the founders' retirements until the Great Depression ended the demand for their atlases. The company was sold to the Franklin Survey Company in 1943, with the name intact, due to its association with quality.

oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:title: Map of Allardt Land Company property and surrounding area, Upper Cumberland Plateau
oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:description: Manuscript map showing south central Kentucky and north central Tennessee, including an area presumed to be the Allardt Land Company property (shown with hatched lines). Map shows towns, creeks, and railroads, including the Tennessee Central Railway, placing the date at no earlier than 1893. Some town names are stamped, some handwritten.

In the late 1800s, Bruno Gernt and M. H. Allardt founded a community of immigrant Germans in the Upper Cumberland Plateau at about the same time the British were settling nearby Rugby. German land agent Gernt envisioned a self-sufficient city here. Gernt sold 9,000 acres owned by the Clarke family of Nebraska in parcels of 25,50, and 200 acres at $4 per acre to farmers, miners, and lumbermen.

oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:title: Scott County, Tennessee
oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:description: Undated hand-drawn map of Scott County, Tennessee, on cloth, using colored inks and pencil. Property owners and rivers and creeks are shown in brown ink. Railroads and related notations are in purple ink. Land entry notations and dates are in pencil. Unidentified blocked-out areas are in blue ink. A mostly legible key is at the top right. This map may have been created for railroad planning and construction. The railroad, the Cincinnati and Southern Railway, was not completed through Scott County until 1879.

Scott County was established in 1849 from parts of Anderson, Campbell, Fentress and Morgan counties. It was named for Mexican War hero General Winfield Scott. Its county seat is Huntsville, while its largest city is Oneida. Scott County was the most strongly opposed county to Tennessee's secession in 1861. It went as far as seceding from Tennessee, and thus the Confederacy, to form the "State of Scott," a resolution that was not repealed until 1986.

oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:title: Hand-drawn map of the United States by German prisoner of war
oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:description: Hand-drawn map of most of the contiguous United States drawn by a German prisoner of war Ruffing. The map includes state borders, some cities, rivers, and railroads. Many state names are spelled phonetically as they would be in German.

Harry Elliott Dudley was born in Corpus Christi, Texas, on July 27, 1895. During World War I he served as sergeant in the United States Marine Corps at its Noncommissioned Officers School at Parris Island, South Carolina. During the interbellum period, Dudley held a number of jobs including a teaching position at the Augusta Military Academy and a brief stint in minor league baseball. He joined the National Guard in 1924. In 1940, his unit was called into active service. From December 1941 until January 1943, he served as Post Inspector and Liaison Officer at Fort Ord. In January 1943, he was transferred to the Office of the Provost Marshal General, which administered internment camps for enemy prisoners of war. In March 1943, he was assigned to the internment camp in Crossville, Tennessee, and eventually made its commanding officer. Dudley retired from the Army in 1954 and died in Sikeston, Missouri, in 1967.

oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:description: World War II newsmap from October 25, 1943 depicting action on various war fronts. Inset maps show the Dnepr River, operations in Burma, Tunisia, and New Guinea. Peterson, Salt Lake City, Fuel pipe lines, Fifth Army engineers, and the Naga Hills of northern Burma.

TSLA holds a large collection of these WWII "newsmaps" detailing for the American public the weekly events of US military efforts in Europe and the Pacific theaters. The Bureau of Public Relations was established in the Office of the Secretary of War in February 1941. The Bureau served as the central War Department agency to determine policies and procedures for disseminating military information to the public. oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:title: Plates 9-10 Sanborn Fire Insurance Map of Nashville, Tenn. (1897, rev. 1911)
oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:description: Plates 9 and 10 from the 1911 revision of the Nashville Sanborn Atlas. These plates depict the neighborhoods just north of the state capitol between 1st Avenue and 5th Avenue and as far north as Jefferson Street. The Nashville Athletic Grounds (Sulphur Dell), sulphur spring, Belleview Public School, Howe Ice Company, and other manufacturing are shown. Grandstands at the baseball stadium had since been torn down to make way for the new one, the first to be named Sulphur Dell. built in 1908. The sulphur spring is the site of the French Lick, the salt lick that attracted hunters to this area for thousands of years.

Daniel Alfred Sanborn, a civil engineer and surveyor, began working on fire insurance maps in the 1860s and his company soon became one of the largest and most successful American map companies. Sanborn's first work mapping cities for insurance purposes began in Tennessee when Aetna Insurance hired him to survey a few towns across the state, however none of these earliest examples are known to exist today (Ristow, Walter W. "United States Fire Insurance and Underwriters Maps· 1852—1968." The Quarterly Journal of the Library of Congress 25, no. 3 (1968): 194-218.). Sanborn maps were originally created to estimate fire insurance risks. Insurance companies would decide how much insurance, if any, was to be offered to a customer solely through the use of a Sanborn map. Today, the maps are frequently used for historical research and for preservation and restoration purposes.

oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:title: Hardin County, Tennessee, Historical Map
oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:description: This hand-drawn colorful map provides rivers, creeks, and areas that were previously occupied by the Chickasaws. In addition, the map offers symbols that indicate the early settlements of the county such as the first school established in Hardin County in 1821, the first church in Hardin County, and the location of the first county seat.

The Jackson Purchase included the area of West Tennessee and southwestern Kentucky between the Tennessee and Mississippi Rivers. This area had historically belonged to the Chickasaws but was ceded in the Treaty of Tecumseh. The treaty with the Chickasaws was negotiated by Andrew Jackson and Issac Shelby in 1818. In 1819, the Jackson Purchase region was opened for settlement and the General Assembly created Hardin County. Hardin County was named after Colonel Joseph Hardin who served as a reprensentative of Washington and Greene counties in the State of Franklin and in the Tennessee Territorial Assembly.

oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:description: Plates 13 and 14 of the 1911 revision of the Sanborn Fire Insurance Atlas of Nashville. These plates depict the area of downtown Nashville from 5th Avenue to 9th Ave. bounded by Cedar and Church streets to the north and south. Includes the Hermitage Hotel, YWCA, YMCA, numerous churches, and the Carnegie Library.

Daniel Alfred Sanborn, a civil engineer and surveyor, began working on fire insurance maps in the 1860s and his company soon became one of the largest and most successful American map companies. Sanborn's first work mapping cities for insurance purposes began in Tennessee when Aetna Insurance hired him to survey a few towns across the state, however none of these earliest examples are known to exist today (Ristow, Walter W. "United States Fire Insurance and Underwriters Maps· 1852—1968." The Quarterly Journal of the Library of Congress 25, no. 3 (1968): 194-218.). Sanborn maps were originally created to estimate fire insurance risks. Insurance companies would decide how much insurance, if any, was to be offered to a customer solely through the use of a Sanborn map. Today, the maps are frequently used for historical research and for preservation and restoration purposes.

oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:title: Proposed extension of Memphis
oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:description: Map of the proposed extension of the city limits of Memphis that accompanied a petition to the Tennessee General Assembly in 1845. The proposed extension would extend the southern border corporation line of Memphis from Union Street to the border of the John Rice and John Ramsey tracts near Beale Street. The Gayoso House, a 19th century hotel is indicated.

The Gayoso House or Gayoso Hotel was named for the Spanish governor of the Natchez District, Manuel Gayoso de Lemos. Gayoso was born in Portugal and fluent in Spanish, English, French, and Latin. His tenure as governor coincided with the establishment of a Spanish fort at the Chickasaw Bluffs, near present-day Memphis. The Hotel was built in 1842. Its location and amenities contributed to its recognition as a premier location in Memphis. The hotel burned down on July 4, 1899, and had to be rebuilt. It operated until 1948 when Goldsmith's department store purchased the building. The second iteration of the hotel still stands as multi-purpose apartments and stores. (A Choctaw Chief and Spanish Governor: Franchimastabé and Manuel Gayoso de Lemos by Charles A. Weeks.) ("Gayoso Hotel" Tennessee Encyclopedia of History and Culture by Blythe Semmer)

oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:title: Die Vereinigten Staaten von Nordamerika, nebst Mexico und Central America
oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:description: German language map of the United States with hand-colored national boundaries. Inset maps of New York City, the Northeast, Panama, Wartburg, San Francisco, and Boston. The map has a nice view of America's newly acquired western territories following the Mexican-American War and the Gadsden Purchase. This map appears to have been produced to encourage German immigration to the United States. Each of the insets contained significant German-speaking communities including Tennessee's Wartburg.

Johann Georg Heck was a German geographer, cartographer, publisher, and bookseller. He was born in Strasbourg around 1795. He served as head of the lithographic department of the Freibourg Art Institute until 1828. He is best known for his Bilder-Atlas zum Conversations-Lexikon. Iconographic Encyclopaedia of Sciences and Arts, which is one of the most popular German-language works of the 19th century. He died on November 20, 1857, in Leipzig.

oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:title: Proposed Tennessee location for superconducting supercollider (SSC)
oai_qdc:qualifieddc.dc:description: Map of the proposed Tennessee location for the Superconducting Supercollider, a massive particle accelerator. Geologists suggested parts of Rutherford, Williamson, Bedford, and Marshall counties to contain the collider, that would have been 53 miles in circumference. Rivers, creeks, roads, towns and county boundaries are all denoted.

In 1987, President Ronald Reagan directed the Department of Energy to request proposals from states to construct a Superconducting Super Collider. The Super Collider was a particle collider designed to smash together subatomic particles to simulate the conditions during the Big Bang. The collider was planned to be a massive oval-shaped tube with a 10 foot wide tunnel, 53 miles in circumference and 14 miles in diameter. Of the 25 states that submitted site proposals, 8 finalists were selected, including Tennessee. The project was estimated to run between $4.4 and $11.8 billion dollars, which included the collider itself, above ground offices, laboratories, and supporting buildings. Ultimately Texas's proposal won out, and construction began in 1993. Cost overruns and political positioning doomed the project and by 1994 the project ended after over $2 billion was already spent. (National Museum of American History Archives, Administrative Note on Superconducting Super Collider Collection) From Department of Economic and Community Development publication.
